subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of moving second reading of Bill C-126. The purpose of this Bill is to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act. The proposed Act will provide the parliamentary authority for Canada's contribution to the International Monetary Fund's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility. It will authorize the Minister of Finance to lend and grant funds to the enhanced structural facility trust on behalf of the Government of Canada. I am very pleased that this morning I will be able to explain this Bill to Members of the House.

The creation of this facility is an important measure taken by the IMF to deal with the debt problems of the world's least developed countries. This mechanism will add significantly to the structural adjustment facility set up in 1986 to help low-income countries balance their payments on very favorable terms.
After the enhanced structural adjustment facility was implemented, the size of the balance of payments problems of the least developed countries led to requests for additional help. It became obvious that international organizations would have to take further special measures to deal with the problems of the poorest debtor countries, especially those of the Sahel. Their extremely slow economic development and the weak growth of their export markets seriously undermined their recovery efforts. Their debt burden had become a major obstacle to their economic development.
Faced with this bleak economic outlook, some developing countries hesitated to pursue or begin sustained adjustment initiatives under the International Monetary Fund. It became obvious that these countries would need increased financial aid on favorable terms to effectively implement through reforms. Although the resources of the structural adjustment facility were limited, they were an appropriate form of assistance because the more favorable terms and extended repayment schedules offered by the structural adjustment facility, as compared to a simple loan, are necessary to help these fragile economies adjust. Increasing the resources of the structural adjustment facility was therefore suggested.

The initiative for an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility received the endorsement of the group of seven

May 20, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
industrialized countries at the Venice Summit in June, 1987. At that time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) expressed Canada's support for such a facility. The result of the international consensus to provide more aid to the poorest debtor countries has been a tripling of the IMF structural adjustment facility. This facility is being enhanced and increased to an important degree.
The Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility is expected to add over $10 billion in equivalent Canadian funds to the resources available through the IMF structural adjustment facility. The loans will carry a subsidized interest rate of one-half per cent per annum and will be repaid over 10 years. The loans are conditional upon countries having an IMF-supported structural reform program in place. The programs will be formulated within a policy framework worked out jointly by the borrowing country, the IMF, and the World Bank. Potentially some 60 very poor countries could benefit from the use of the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility resources.
The Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility contributions are made to two accounts. The contributions to the loan account will earn interest. Contributions to the subsidy account will be in the form of grants and allow the IMF to lend loan account funds at one-half per cent interest per year. The Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility has received the enthusiastic support of the international community. Some 25 countries have made pledges to this facility.
In Canada's case, the Bill before us will give the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the authority to lend up to $550 million Canadian to the loan account. These moneys will be lent in three equal instalments over three years beginning in 1988. This contribution will pay Canada a rate of interest based on long-term rates for domestic financial instruments of five major world currencies.
The legislation will further allow for the Minister of Finance to grant up to $250 million Canadian over the 12-year life of the trust, in order that our loan contribution can be loaned out to low-income countries at one-half per cent interest per year. Canada's contribution will be financed through the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The subsidy portion will be counted as part of Canada's official development assistance. The legislation allows changes to both the subsidy and loan contributions, through Order-in-Council, to reflect future international discussions.
As a Government we support the structural adjustment facility because we believe that countries that are undertaking necessary adjustments in their economic policies deserve the encouragement of the international community. This is particularly true when required policy reforms may be politically unpopular in the short term. Furthermore, the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility will be complementary to our bilateral aid efforts. The economic stabilization of the least developed economies, quite frankly, is a necessary prerequisite to their more effective use of bilateral aid.
For all those reasons, this Bill deserves our strong support.

subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-126, an Act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act.
As has been said, this legislation gives authority to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to contribute to the International Monetary Fund in support of the new IMF balance of payments assistance program, the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility or ESAF.
ESAF is a trust fund established by the International Monetary Fund to make resources available to some of the poorest highly indebted countries. When I talk of some of the poorest countries, Mr. Speaker, I am talking about countries where the average per capita income is $300 a year.
The resources that are being planned for now will support policy programs that help their balance of payments, because these poorest countries are among the most heavily indebted, and enable them to start planning for economic growth.
ESAF was initiated at the June, 1987, Venice Summit of industrialized countries. At the summit it was agreed that the magnitude of the debt problem, and the protracted nature of the balance of payments problem of the poorest countries called for additional resources.
ESAF will operate on the basis of two accounts. The loan account will pay contributors, that is, the industrialized countries, a market rate of interest. The grant account, or the subsidy account, will be composed of grants which allow loans to be made to the borrowing countries at .5 per cent interest per annum for 10 years with 5 years' grace. As has been said, ESAF will support the adjustment efforts of about 60 low-income countries, many of which are in sub-Saharan Africa.
Canada will support this initiative by providing loans at concessional interest rates to these poor or debt-ridden countries, conditional on the countries putting in place the structural adjustment and growth programs which will help them achieve economic self-sufficiency. Perhaps I could say here that some of the commercial lending in the 1970s was not sufficiently buttressed by performance requirements or by assistance to these countries, to improve their lot.
The ESAF, in contrast, is planned as an initiative to encourage policy reform in developing countries. It will allow the very poor, debt-ridden countries, to maintain needed imports while servicing their foreign debt obligations and undertaking policy reforms. Of course, it offers an opportunity for further co-operation between the IMF, the World Bank and the developing countries.
The following are the amounts that are being contributed by some other countries in special drawing rights converted into Canadian dollars: Japan, approximately $3.7 billion to the loan account and approximately $510 million to the subsidy account; West Germany, approximately $1,190 million to the loan account and approximately $221 million to the subsidy
May 20, 1988

account; France, $1,360 million to the loan account and $1,190 million to the subsidy account.
As I said earlier, a poor country to be assisted under this program is defined as a country where the average annual per capita income is $300. Many of these countries are indeed in dire straits because simply meeting the interest rate on their foreign debts takes up almost all of their GDP, leaving them unable to undertake planning to get out of their basic predicament and to improve the economy of their country.
Prior to 1982, low-income countries experienced external pressures similar to those experienced by middle-income countries. Two of these were the commodity booms of the 1970s and the two oil shocks that led to huge increases in the price of oil. The cruel world-wide recession of 1981 and 1982, of course, exacerbated the problems.
Low-income countries which import their energy were faced with high energy import costs after 1973. New sources of funds were acquired to sustain the growth that had been stimulated by the expanded commodity exports of 1971. The traditional source of funds, official development assistance, was not meeting the needs of low-income countries. These countries began to look to commercial banks seeking to recycle OPEC surpluses. The result was, in the years between 1972 and 1982, a striking shift toward capital market and nonconcessional debt occurring in low-income countries. The commercial banks have to bear some responsibility for this. They looked at short-term credit worthiness. They did not look at the fact that these countries had serious problems that needed to be addressed which went far beyond their need for immediate loans.
According to a World Bank study, borrowings from the private financial markets increased ten-fold from 1972 to 1979. As interest rates began to rise rapidly, debt servicing became an enormous problem for the poorest countries, compounded by the fact that new commercial financing abruptly declined. Making matters worse, of course, were the underlying inefficient domestic policies in place in low-income countries. For some of these countries weapons imports add a costly drain, absorbing capital that could have been spent on programs to develop economic growth.
The scenario for some of these countries is bleak. On a per capita basis the debt for the low-income countries is higher than that of middle-income Latin American countries. Their debt has grown faster and is a heavier burden. Most of these countries lack the most basic infrastructure and personnel to put in place needed reforms.
Many of these countries over-borrowed but did not make the necessary domestic structural domestic adjustments. In terms of the international financial system, the smaller debtor countries do not pose a threat. But in human terms the poverty, the starvation, are a constant source of distress. Hence this particular measure is welcome, provided that it is carefully monitored.
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
Canada must ensure that the financial assistance is given in a context that involves the recipient country in defining its needs, in planning, and some appropriate expectations for change must be set.
When I spoke in the House on March 12, 1985, also on an amendment to the Bretton Woods Act, I pointed out that while financial assistance is desperately needed by the poor countries of the world, financial assistance without performance requirements and monitoring will lead to inefficient investment.
The commercial lenders simply evaluated the credit worthiness of the borrowers for short-term loans but failed to monitor how the funds were used, or the long-term policies and prospects of the borrowing countries. Bilateral country-to-country assistance is very often given without insisting on the restructuring that would lead that country out of the need for assistance to the same extent. This is understandable because sovereign nations do not easily accept attempts by other countries to influence or dictate their policies. However, an international organization such as the IMF is in a position to discuss with recipient countries their plans, to help them set appropriate targets. This is a most important part of the aid and a very necessary condition of what we are agreeing to this morning.
The multilateral financial institutions have a better opportunity to design and evaluate adjustment programs in cooperation with the recipient country and in ways that are acceptable to all concerned.
In April, 1984, I heard the Vice-President of the World Bank speaking in Lisbon on the issue of conditional aid to developing countries. He talked about conditionality implying hard choices and disagreements. He also pointed out that major reforms can only take place if they are implemented gradually over a number of years and financed in parallel with closely monitored implementation. One can hardly emphasize too much the need for co-operation and full partnership with the recipient country. This is the key.
Imposing harsh conditions without consultation, understanding and agreement of the assisted country is fruitless. It only makes for resentment and lack of co-operation. The role that the IMF must play is that of the consultant who studies and evaluates the needs of the country, makes recommendations on policy and helps the recipient country meet those recommendations.
Canada must ensure that this happens. Canada is particularly well suited to do so. Our officials have a reputation for being able to be helpful without taking over. It is important that this continue.
Efficient and thoughtful long-term planning and implementation will benefit both the assisted and assisting countries. As

May 20, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
developing countries are able to improve their economies, they will depend less on assistance from countries like Canada.
My Party is basically in agreement with the principle of this Bill. Indeed, no one who has travelled in some of the very poor countries can fail to be moved by the dreadful conditions-the starvation, the lack of opportunity for people to achieve their potential, to achieve basic education. We clearly have a duty to help and the average Canadian is glad to do so and have tax dollars invested in this. However, Canadians want to know that the Government is fully committed to ensuring that the $800 million being committed today to assist the poorest countries is wisely and constructively used.
In fact, no new money has actually been committed. The $250 million grant will come from the current development aid envelope. The remainder is loans at market rates.
I should also point out that discussion of Third World loans is on the agenda of the summit meeting in June in Toronto and this could be an opportunity for Canada to propose new initiatives and also to work toward better international understanding and more effective use of the moneys being committed at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to Bill C-126 dealing with an amendment to the Bretton Woods Act and other agreements. While this very short Bill appears to be very straightforward, since it deals with the debt load of the poorest countries in the world we believe it needs more than simply a cursory debate. We do not want to hold the Bill up unduly, but we do want to focus attention on the debt problem. We hope to be able to hear witnesses and make amendments in committee.
The Bill provides both for the loan and the granting of funds to the International Monetary Fund in order to fund: "Any trust or body established by the Fund". A sum of $550 million is the total mentioned for the loan, and $250 million for the grant. However, in both cases the amount can be increased by the Governor in Council. In other words, the Government is asking for a blank cheque.
The immediate purpose for these funds is to meet Canada's commitment to the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility.
When the Bill states: "Any trust or body established by the IMF", it is more open-ended than necessary for the purposes of Canada's commitment. I think it is more open-ended than this House of Commons should allow and I hope it can be strengthened in committee.
The Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility originated last June at the Venice Summit as an attempt by the industrialized world to come to grips with the debt problem, particularly the debt problem of the poorest countries in the world and the balance of payment problems of the poorest countries, most of which are in Africa.
The IMF has now taken this under its wing and hopes to provide some $6 billion special drawing rights, which would be the equivalent of just over $10 billion Canadian.
The Government hand-out on the Bill states that these resources will support policy reforms designed to restore balance of payments sustainability and enable these countries to maintain satisfactory economic growth. Taken in isolation, the terms of the proposed loans to the poor countries are extremely generous, almost unbelievable. Certainly 0.5 per cent interest per annum for 10 years, with five years' grace, is extremely generous.
However, the great portion of the contribution from Canada and other countries will be used to subsidize this negligible rate of interest so that the original lenders will get a normal rate of interest on the loan portion. That is, the grant portion will be used to subsidize the interest portion so that there will be a market rate of interest paid.
We support this concessional flow of funds, but we do question the so-called policy reforms which the IMF will impose on the recipient countries. That is the burden of a good deal of our debate this morning. It should be noted that a good part of the funds will be used to service debts owed to the same countries that are lending the money, or to multinational agencies like the IMF itself. In other words, ESAF will be used not to meet the developmental needs of the poorest countries but to help keep them from defaulting to First World creditors.
The World Bank has estimated that the total debt of developing countries is something like $1.19 trillion U.S. This could be a considerable under-estimate since the World Bank tends to take very conservative estimates of such things as debt. This has climbed from a $1 trillion debt just two or three years ago.
Much of the attention about this debt and most of the anxiety has focused on big debtors such as Brazil or Mexico, both of which owe over $100 billion in U.S. funds.
Indeed, the six largest problem debtors account for 32 per cent of the $1.19 trillion. Their inability to service these debts creates major problems not only for themselves but for the entire world economy.
This problem is outside the range of ESAF, but it should not be outside the range of our concerns in the House. I know it will not be outside the concerns of the economic summit in Toronto next month.
It is outside the range of concern of ESAF because these are far from the poorest countries. ESAF is designed to help countries like the sub-Saharan countries of Africa, which account for 5.2 per cent of this total debt. In contrast to countries owing large debts to private banks, most of the subSaharan and African countries' debt is official. Only 13.5 per cent is owed to banks or to private creditors. Sixty-two per cent of that debt is owed to OECD bilateral countries or to multilateral creditors, and smaller amounts are owed to OPEC
May 20, 1988

and Soviet bloc countries. While these countries may have lower debts in terms of the absolute numbers, these debts are horrendous in terms of their relation to the Gross National Product per capita or expressed in terms of the ratio of debt exports.
I would like to quote from Roy Culpeper's study for the North-South Institute called The Debt Matrix in which he looks at some selected low income sub-Saharan debtors. Benin had in 1985 a GNP per capita of $260 U.S. and a total external debt of $890 million U.S. The ratio of debt to export of goods and services in 1986 was 321.6 per cent. Gambia had a GNP per capita of $230 U.S. It owes $270 million U.S. and has a debt export ratio of 290.5 per cent. Liberia had a GNP per capita of $470 U.S. It owes $1,303 billion and has a ratio of debt to export of goods and services of 280.8 per cent. Madagascar has a GNP per capita of $240 U.S. It owes $2,899 billion U.S. and has a debt export ratio of 708.4 per cent. Mauritania had a GNP per capita of $420 U.S. and owes $1,761 billion. It has a debt capita ratio of 387.1 per cent. Senegal has a per capita of $370 U.S. GNP. It owes $2,989 billion and has a debt export ratio of 302.2 per cent. Sudan has a GNP per capita of $300 U.S. and owes $8,272 billion. It has an astounding debt export ratio of $1,145.7. Tanzania, with a per capita GNP of $290, owes $3,955 billion. It has a debt export ratio of $864.4.
Zaire, with a very low GNP per capita of only $170 U.S., owes $5,430 billion. It has a debt export ratio of 266.8 per cent. Zambia has a GNP per capita of $390 U.S. and owes $5,300 billion. It has a debt export ratio of 326.1 per cent.
When we look at these figures and do not just think of them as dry statistics but look at the reality that here we have countries with Gross National Products per capita of $200, $300 and $400 each, with these astounding debts we can well ask how can they ever service them, let alone pay them off. Culpeper points out that for developing countries in total the debt export ratio deteriorated from 169 per cent in 1982 to 227 per cent in 1986. Zambia provides a tragic example of what this means for an individual developing country.
Let me refer to Roger Young's study called Zambia Adjusting to Poverty. He points out that the outstanding short and long-term debt now stands at four times the estimated dollar value of the Gross Domestic Product as at the end of 1986. The schedule debt servicing ratio in 1987 stands at nearly 100 per cent of estimated exports, and if arrears are included at 150 per cent of exports, interest payments alone in 1986 were estimated at $336 million U.S. or 35 per cent of exports.
At present Zambia is in arrears both to the IMF and the World Bank and is ineligible to resource the general funds of the IMF. As a result of this horrendous situation, the real Gross Domestic Product per person has fallen 19 per cent since 1981 or 3 per cent per year in each of the past six years. This
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
has meant a very drastic deterioration in the country's social infrastructure in health, education and housing as these have become more expensive and more inaccessible. In order to get help from the IMF, countries have to adjust their economies to meet IMF conditions. These conditions are imposed upon Third World countries from a western monetarist point of view and they usually have the following components.
They usually involve devaluation of local currency so that the local currency will not buy as much as it previously did, and cut-backs in government services. This means cut-backs in health services and education, lay-offs of government employees, which increases the unemployment in countries that are already suffering from up to 40 per cent unemployment, and it means raising the price of food, hitting particularly hard at the poor. The elimination of subsidies for state-run enterprises means opening the local economy to outside investment and control. Nevertheless, in the last few years, faced with these very difficult situations, at least 28 African countries have introduced measures along these lines.
As I pointed out, these measures hit particularly hard at the poor and cause a great deal of social unrest. Zambia is a case in point. In order to receive international help, it raised the price of maize meal by 125 per cent. When the price of the staple food is raised it causes great hardship for the poor. Riots resulted and 17 people were killed. President Kenneth Kaunda was forced to rescind the price increase and broke off the IMF program. As I pointed out earlier, Zambia is not now eligible for regular IMF funding.
It is interesting to note that when the Senate of Canada was studying the international financial institutions and the debt problem of developing countries, Mr. Cedric Ritchie, Chairman of the Bank of Nova Scotia, told the committee that continual application of austerity measures "have exacted a social and political cost that in some countries at least appear to be unsustainable. Mr. William Mulholland, Chairman of the Bank of Montreal, put it even more directly, "If we think we can convince debtor countries that it is in their interest to eat less in order to make low repayments, we better think again". These are chairmen of large Canadian banks, banks which themselves are heavily involved in the whole debt problem, but they recognize that simply tightening the screws on poor people will not work.
An international labour organization report points out that these measures do not work in many poor countries which lack a strong industrial base where unemployment and malnutrition are already very high. The programs may have reduced the balance of payments deficit, but they have not led to economic recovery. That is why Africa is in such a difficult situation today.
Western liberal democracies have often been very critical of the poor human rights record of many African countries. We have good reason to be concerned about the human rights

May 20, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
records of those countries, but we need also recognize that we share a good deal of the blame. If the IMF, controlled by the West, imposes such onerous conditions on African countries that they lead to higher food costs, more hungry children, less schooling, poor health facilities and higher unemployment, do we wonder if this will cause social unrest that will lead to riots and do we wonder if in response, Governments take stern measures to put these riots down?
The point is that IMF programs, far from leading to recovery for African and other poor nations, often seem to pave the road to increased poverty, social chaos and the breakdown of democracy. It is important not to exaggerate at this point. African nations themselves admit that many of their problems are the result of mistakes they made in the past. Some of their reforms are necessary, and these reforms form the basis for their program of recovery that was adopted by African nations at the special session of the United Nations in 1987.
Having admitted this, we need to realize the truth of what Julius Nyerere, the President of Tanzania, said in 1984 about the IMF and the World Bank. He said:
These institutions, originally meant as institutions of co-operation among
the developed countries, are now being used as instruments of control over the
developing countries. They have become instruments for a new kind of empire.
They are being used as instruments of power to dominate the Third World.
The rigid IMF policy has meant that in 1987, debtor countries paid $5.9 billion more back to the IMF than they received from it. We are talking about poor countries here. We are talking about the plight of poverty in these countries. We are talking about the IMF providing some help to them, yet in 1987, according to a Globe and Mail article of February 2 of this year, they paid back to the IMF $5.9 billion more than they received. This $5.9 billion U.S. is coming from poverty-stricken African countries.
Admittedly, in recent months, the International Monetary Fund has begun to show some sensitivity to the impact of its policies on poor people. Michael Camdessus, the new head of the IMF, wants to ease the monitoring provisions for loans and he supports contingency financing for countries with reform packages that face unexpected shocks such as a collapse in commodity prices or a rapid rise in interest rates.
As one Third World person put it, these measures are welcome, but he asked if they are enough and if they are coming in time to prevent a complete collapse in many of these countries.
Combined with the debt problem, we need to recognize that African countries face a decline in the level of official development assistance from many countries. Canada plays a very ambiguous role here. When the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) appeared before the United Nations in 1984, he promised that Canada would reach its goal of 0.7 per cent of GNP by 1990. With the cut-backs the Government has introduced, that was reduced to 0.7 per cent by 1995. In another Budget, it was said that we would reach
that figure sometime in the 21st century, and in the meantime, we would try to reach the goal of 0.6 per cent by the year 1995-96.
The Special Joint Committee on Canada's External Relations that was chaired by the Hon. Minister responsible for this Bill two years ago recommended that we go back to the original commitment of reaching 0.7 per cent of GNP by 1990. The Government rejected that. Then, when the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade studied the whole question of the amount of our development assistance last year, the committee, with a Conservative majority, recommended that we should move at least more quickly to the 0.6 per cent goal. The committee report read:
With such a floor securely in place, we believe Canada should make steady progress towards higher aid targets. We doubt that the current plan to hold the ratio steady at 0.5 per cent until 1990 and then increase it sharply to 0.6 per cent in the following five years is realistic, particularly considering that we are now at a level slightly below 0.5 per cent. We are concerned that Canada may find itself once more in the position of abandoning its commitments.
In the Committee's view, a plan is needed that would take us to the 0.6 per cent level in 1995-96 by steady, achievable annual increments. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that progress towards achieving the 0.6 per cent target in 1995-96 should begin in the 1988-1989 fiscal year, rather than the current plan of fiscal year 1990-91, and proceed by steady annual increases. We estimate that would bring the ODA/GNP ratio to 0.53 per cent in fiscal year 1990-91.
Unfortunately, the Government chose to ignore that advice as well.
Canada's record is not bad when compared with that of countries like the United Kingdom or the United States, but it is not good when compared with some of the Nordic countries or when compared with the record of the need for development assistance.
The real villain is the fall in commodity prices. Unfortunately, the International Monetary Fund is much more ready to move to prop up the monetary system than it is to put in place some system of price stabilization that would result in commodity prices not being subject to the wild fluctuations that they are so that development countries would not be constantly the victim of international markets.
Roy Culpeper, in his book Forced Adjustment, again a North-South study, pointed out that sub-Saharan Africa went from being the export growth leader of the world from 1965 to 1980 to being the world lagger, with exports shrinking at an annual rate of 5 per cent during 1980-85. He points out that in 1986, the terms of trade of developing countries fell by some 16.8 per cent, equivalent to a loss in exports of about $100 billion. However, because of the growth in the volume of exports, developing countries' export purchasing power fell only by about 10 per cent.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN EMPLOYMENT CENTRE FOR DRUMMOND STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to urge students who are looking for a summer job to register as soon as possible with the Canada Employment Centre for Students in Drummond.
And I invite the people of Drummond, whether they are manufacturers, merchants, farmers or private citizens, to help make the Employment Centre for Students a success by hiring quality manpower. High school, CEGEP and university students are counting on the community to help them find jobs.
So far, 211 applications have been approved in my riding under the Challenge 88 Program. These projects will create 322 jobs, thanks to federal wage subsidies totalling $414,507. The program demonstrates how keen this Government is to help young people make the transition from school to the labour market.
I am very proud that I can help create jobs for the students in Drummond through this program set up by the Conservative Government.
I wish all young people in my riding the best of luck with their job search, and I urge them once again to register without delay with the Drummond Canada Employment Centre.

subtopic: RUMOURED TRANSFER OF TRAIN REGULATION CONTROL CENTRE FROM MONTREAL TO TORONTO
RUMOURED TRANSFER OF TRAIN REGULATION CONTROL CENTRE FROM MONTREAL TO TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
yesterday I received a request from about 100 CN employees to intervene in a situation which they reject as unacceptable, and it was in connection with rumours that the Switching and Control Centre will move from Montreal to Toronto. In fact, these people are employed as telegraph operators and in addition to the threat of cutbacks at CN, they will also have to cope with this possibility, which may deprive them of a chance

to switch to other jobs such as train dispatcher or director of train operations in Montreal.
The move to Toronto will leave these employees no alternative except unemployment, since their jobs will then be filled by other employees located in Toronto.
I don't think we are giving them a fair break. Some of their positions are being cut, and at the same time they may be deprived of a chance to get another job with CN. If Montreal is not going to get the space agency, Mr. Speaker, couldn't we at least keep the railways?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with the Government's decision to make the West Memorial Building at 344 Wellington Street in Ottawa the new home of the National Archives and to consolidate the housing of its collections in a special facility to be built in the future.
The National Archives contain 250,000 Yousuf Karsh's negatives, Marshall McLuhan's complete works and papers, and a set of Frances Ann Hopkins' paintings of the fur trade. It also houses over 60 million manuscripts, the personal papers of past Prime Ministers of Canada, and over one million maps and architectural drawings. There are also 70,000 hours of sound recordings in the Archives' collections.
The proposed environmentally controlled storage facility will better enable archivists to preserve existing collections and make room for the Archives to collect more of Canada's precious national heritage.
The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) based her decision on the report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. This is a good example of how this Government responds to committee recommendations.
This Government cares about our national heritage.

maintopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL OF MOOSE AND MEMBERS
NATIONAL CAPITAL OF MOOSE AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a tough week in Parliament for Members on all sides. We have had abortion, free trade, and the Meech Lake constitutional resolution, all of which are big, tough issues. However, let us not lose sight of the sweeter side of life. Remember, this is the week when a moose fell into the

May 20, 1988
swimming pool of a suburban Ottawa home. What could be more Canadian? Could that happen in any other capital city of the world?
Tonight is the opening of the magnificent new National Gallery here in Ottawa. That gives us a chance to reflect on the vital role our museums and art galleries play in lifting our spirits, educating our young people, and reflecting our past and present in all their diversity. Therefore, I propose a toast with my glass of water to Ottawa, to Canada, to the new National Gallery, and to us at the end of a tough week!

maintopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL OF MOOSE AND MEMBERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I bring to the attention of all Members of this House a very important event on the nation's annual calendar, Canada's Fitweek. This year's event starts today, Sneaker Day, and will run until May 29.

During the next ten days, Mr. Speaker, one out of three Canadians will take part in Canada's Fitweek, the biggest celebration of physical activity in the world.
Thousands of organizers and volunteers have planned nearly 14,000 events that will take place in schools and communities across this country.

This phenomenal program is co-ordinated jointly by the Government of Canada through the efforts of Fitness Canada, along with the 12 provincial and territorial Governments and 20 national fitness and recreation agencies.

Finally, under the slogan " Celebrate Good Times", the whole country will be moving, from May 20 to 29, and I invite all of you to join in.

So let us see those sneakers!

Mr. Speaker, did you know that acid rain is eating away at our houses? Acid rain is not only corroding our monuments and
destroying our lakes and forests, it is also gradually destroying the houses people live in.
In Canada acid rain damage is heaviest in Ontario and Quebec. Martin Weaver, an Ottawa conservation consultant, said recently that masonry in Montreal is crumbling, metalwork is corroding, and paint is fading and peeling at up to twice the expected rate. He added that construction materials once thought to last almost forever, like granite, concrete, and marble, are being reduced to spongy masses that can be cut like cheese with a blunt knife. This is really bad news. The situation is alarming now and getting worse every day.
Some questions beg to be asked. What can be done to stop the effect of acid rain on houses? What is the Government doing about it? Why is it so weak vis-a-vis our neighbour to the south? Our growing aging population have only limited funds for the upkeep of their homes. Who will help them with their repair bills? The problem is urgent and will not go away. The solution rests squarely on the shoulders of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

subtopic: PLANNED EXPANSION TO INCLUDE TRADE SHOW
PLANNED EXPANSION TO INCLUDE TRADE SHOW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my riding of Fraser Valley East, in beautiful British Columbia, has been proud to be the home of the Abbotsford Airshow for the last 27 years. The Airshow will expand in 1989 to include an aerospace trade show, thanks to a $3.4 million contribution cost-shared equally by our federal Government and the Province of British Columbia. This will make the Abbotsford Airshow and the new trade show comparable with the famous Paris and Farnborough Airshows in Europe.
The funding, welcomed by all involved in the Airshow, comes from the Western Diversification Fund and the B.C. Ministry of Economic Development.
Airshow Canada, as the trade show will be called, will be devoted to aircraft, space aviation components, and the latest powered flight technology. It will also be a forum for international decision-makers and aviation business leaders and in no way will diminish the thrills and chills of the Airshow.
Congratulations, Abbotsford International Airshow, for a job well done! Fraser Valley East and the rest of Canada look forward to an even more successful and interesting airshow and trade show in the future. Come see us the second week in August. It's well worth the trip.
May 20, 1988

subtopic: TREATMENT OF IMMIGRANT WOMEN DOMESTIC WORKERS
TREATMENT OF IMMIGRANT WOMEN DOMESTIC WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government legislates semi-slave labour for some women. Because women's work in Canada gets less than two-thirds of men's pay and housework less still, immigrant domestics are imported to work at about $10,000 per year.
There are no real limits on their hours so we cannot say how much they get per hour. They must usually live in and are subject to traditional abuse by either man or woman in the house. They are compelled by our federal law to stay in that occupation for two or three years in what one immigration official called a "halfway house".
Why do they come here? They are hoping to be landed. What are their chances? In order to stay more than two or three years they must leave domestic work and upgrade themselves by study for work that would be accepted as another category of immigration. Often they cannot get the time to study. Many are forced to return home to be replaced by others on the same treadmill.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall), who is also the Minister responsible for women, ought to revise the regulations so as to free these semi-slave labouring women.

Mr. Speaker, Alberta food processors look increasingly to export markets for their products. The drive to export fine processed food products is southward and westward. The markets in the United States are opening to Alberta food. The Pacific Rim nations such as Japan, Taiwan, Korea and Singapore are developing a taste for Alberta beef, for Alberta smoked trout, for Alberta foodstuffs of quality and nourishment.
The free trade agreement, and Canada's commitment to GATT, combined with Alberta hustle, all work together to provide food exports to make millions of mouths water.
Food processing is the second largest Alberta industry. In our drive to diversity, let's make it number one.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-ENVIRONMENTAL IMPLICATIONS
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-ENVIRONMENTAL IMPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday at the examination of the current estimates of Environment Canada, I learned with shock and dismay that Environment Canada has not conducted any study on the environmental implications of the Canada-U.S. trade deal. This is astonishing considering the fact that in January, 1986, the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council, at the request of the Minister, strongly recommended that it will be necessary to examine the environmental implications just as systematically as the economic ones. This has not been done.
By contrast, most other federal Departments have studied the deal's impact on their areas of responsibility and have even publicly reported on potential impacts. The deal contains provisions such as Schedule 7 on pesticides and their regulation which will undoubtedly have an impact on the environment.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has been remiss in his duty and responsibility. He should have studied the trade deal from the environmental point of view so as to determine its long-term consequences for our natural resources.

Mr. Speaker, the bank service charge hearings are over but the letters continue to arrive. Customers are now being levied service charges even when the banks make an error. In one case a cheque was written for $6 and was returned as NSF. The writer of the cheque was charged $12.50 for writing the NSF cheque. The recipient of the cheque was charged $4 for depositing the NSF cheque.
Upon investigation, it turned out that there were sufficient funds to cover the cheque in the first place, so the first bank cheerfully refunded the $12.50 service charge. However, the depositor's bank refused to reverse its $4 service charge since, according to it, a charge is levied on all returned cheques.
Banks should be prohibited from levying service charges on people who are victims of NSF cheques, but even more fundamentally, banks should be prohibited from levying service charges which result from bank errors in the first place.

May 20, 1988

maintopic: S. O. 21 FORESTRY LEGENDARY STAND OF SITKA SPRUCE-CALL FOR PRESERVATION
S. O. 21 FORESTRY LEGENDARY STAND OF SITKA SPRUCE-CALL FOR PRESERVATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, Queen Beatrix of The Netherlands concluded her Canadian tour by watching loggers fall a 900-year old Douglas Fir near Duncan on Vancouver Island. Over six feet through and nearly 200 feet high, this giant took only seven minutes to fall. Nine hundred years to grow, seven minutes to fall!
Pretty soon we will not have any of these giants left to show visiting Royalty or anyone else. For this reason I commend McMillan-Bloedel for placing a one-month moratorium on the building of a road into the Carmanah Creek area where we have a legendary stand of spruce only now becoming known. Thought to be the largest Sitka Spruce in Canada, perhaps in the world, these trees should be protected from the power saw.
During the one-month moratorium, I urge federal and provincial Governments to work together with McMillan-Bloedel and the people of British Columbia and Canada to ensure this priceless treasure is preserved. Perhaps the grandchildren of Queen Beatrix, as well as our own grandchildren, might want to come and see them still standing.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is a trading nation, and has been since the fur traders sold their wares to the Hudson Bay Company. Today, however, we no longer depend totally on our natural resources for trade. In fact, for the first time in our history, our economy has boomed during a period of low resource prices.
Canadian companies earn more export dollars from the sales of insurance policies than they do from softwood lumber or crude oil. We export more office equipment than meat. Canadian exports of wheat are now worth only half as much as our exports of trucks. More than two-thirds of our exports are manufactured goods.
Trade is Canada's future. It is the Canadian way, yesterday, today, and tomorrow, and into the 21st century. Those who oppose free trade oppose the future prosperity of Canada. Are you listening, Mr. Peterson?

Mr. Speaker, Wednesday was International Museums Day and this year Canada marks that celebration with the opening of the doors of our world-class new National Gallery. One hundred and eight years after its establishment, the National Gallery finally has a home worthy of its collection. Congratulations to Canadian architect Moshe Safdie for his creative design and use of daylight, making it not only a refreshing place to view art but an architectural masterpiece in its own right.
Never before was so much of the gallery's collection of 40,000 works of art on display. In the Canadian historical section, more space means that the number of pieces on display has been doubled from 375 to almost 800.
Amidst these celebrations we salute the Liberal Party, whose foresight started the ball rolling for this Canadian cultural landmark.
Canadian museums play a unique role in furthering public education as well as in the preservation and display of the collection of our heritage. We are all looking forward to full discussion with all museums on the new federal museum policy.

subtopic: CALL FOR TIMELY RENT PAYMENTS IN NORTHERN AREAS
CALL FOR TIMELY RENT PAYMENTS IN NORTHERN AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a standard clause in lease agreements entered into by the Government of Canada as lessee, states that the rent will be paid on the last day of each and every month during the term thereof. However, it is not uncommon for rent cheques to be a week or more late in coming to my constituency. An explanation often given is that: "We are not just set up to make timely payments in the North".
The lessor is obliged to keep to the terms of the agreement and so should the lessee. Perhaps Public Works Canada could work a little harder to ensure timely payment of rent cheques in northern areas.

Mr. Speaker, this Sunday is National Missing Childrens' Day. Last year, with much fanfare, the Government brought in the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act which was
May 20, 1988

supposed to help families locate missing children. However, in my own community I have now received a very solid example of how it is not working.
I refer specifically to the abduction of Ryan Kevin Johnston, aged three and a half years. He was abducted by his father on January 28, 1988. Mr. Johnston abducted the child and has essentially disappeared from the face of the earth. The access that has been sought to federal and provincial records has been very slow in coming.
It took four months to find out from the federal data bank that no new address has been posted. In fact the legislation prohibits access to information under the Income Tax Act. It is funny that the Income Tax Act will allow us to get an address of a tax evader but it will not allow us to get an address of a person who abducts a child. Nothing could be more heinous than the abduction of a child and I think we should change the Income Tax Act to ensure that people who steal children are dealt with under the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, on April 21, the federal Government in the person of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret), announced the Conservative Government's decision to participate in the U.S. space station. At the time, the Minister guaranteed that 35 per cent of the contracts would be for Quebec and 35 per cent for Ontario. Unfortunately, this morning we heard that so far, Ontario has obtained 77.8 per cent and Quebec a meagre 17.9 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, at this rate, pretty soon all the contracts will have been awarded, and by the time the Government announces the space agency will be located in Montreal, it will be an empty shell. There will be nothing left to give, since Ontario will have the lion's share!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-P.E.I. POTATO AND LOBSTER EXPORTS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-P.E.I. POTATO AND LOBSTER EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister for International Trade mocked the Hon. Member for Egmont when that Hon. Member attempted to find out from the Minister why Prince Edward Island lobster fishermen and potato farmers were the
Oral Questions
last minute victims of the Prime Minister's trade deal with the United States. I want to say to him that this Government seems to revel in picking on the little guy.
Why, in this instance, is the Government allowing Canada's smallest province to become a victim of the continuing changes of attitude of the Americans on this trade deal? The Prime Minister is so concerned about the deal that he really doesn't care what happens to anything else.
What is the Minister for International Trade actually prepared to do in response to American action on lobsters and potatoes which, as he knows, undermines the economy of Prince Edward Island and, indeed, of the Atlantic provinces? Aside from the bombast, what is he actually prepared to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-P.E.I. POTATO AND LOBSTER EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it ill behooves the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to talk about bombast when he has threatened to tear up an agreement entered into by the U.S. and Canada. He is the world's leading expert on bombast.
With respect to the question about P.E.I., first, on the issue of potatoes, we continually hear the Opposition crying wolf. What happened with respect to potatoes? The U.S. Senate Finance Committee has proposed that their legislation provide the President with authority to negotiate bilateral quantitative limitations on potato trade with Canada. All it is is that they want to give the President authority to negotiate.
The President can negotiate, but it takes two sides to enter into an agreement. There is nothing objectionable in that, surely. It is a recommendation to the administration that they negotiate. So much for the potato threat. We are not going to agree to anything that will limit the export of potatoes from Canada to the United States.
With respect to lobsters, the United States, I might tell the Hon. Leader of the Opposition, and pass the message on to Premier Ghiz, introduced new federal legislation on lobster carapace size in 1987. Under the regulations the minimum size would increase to three and seven thirty-second inches this year, and so on.
An industry-government meeting was held in Charlottetown on this subject on May 15 with respect to the impact of these regulations on the Canadian lobster fishery. Governments were represented, as were industry and the fishermen. All provincial government representatives, with the exception of the Quebec representative, supported a carapace size increase. The situation is a little bit different than the public impression given. In addition, this is a regulation already made by the U.S. federal authorities.
With respect to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and the language suggested to be added by the committee members several days ago, we are protesting that. We do not think that it has any place in this legislation. We are delivering

May 20, 1988
Oral Questions
a note of protest. We will act vigorously in the interest of Canada.
Let us note that a meeting was held on May 15. The government representatives there supported an increase in the minimum size.
I might further point out that the P.E.I. industry is largely a canner fishery which is not affected by the U.S. regulations.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-P.E.I. POTATO AND LOBSTER EXPORTS
speechtext: Time!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-P.E.I. POTATO AND LOBSTER EXPORTS
speechtext: These are the facts. If the hon. gentleman wants to talk about bombast, he better examine his own bombastic statements.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-P.E.I. POTATO AND LOBSTER EXPORTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to encourage the Minister to go on as he has. He has become the best salesman that we have on this side of the House to sink this deal.
Hear, hear!

What the Minister is really saying is: "No problem with potatoes. No problem with lobsters. But we sent a note of diplomatic protest because it goes against the spirit of the deal". Of course it goes against the spirit of the deal.
There are really two issues at stake here. One is the Prime Minister's willingness to sell out everything and anything to keep this deal intact. The other is a question of the Government's honesty in treating this deal in the House of Commons.
Why did the Minister for International Trade yesterday in answer to the Hon. Member for Egmont say that there was no problem with respect to lobsters or potatoes when he had already sent a diplomatic note to the United States, as he revealed outside the House? Why did he not come clean with the House of Commons at that time and say: "Yes, there is a problem. Yes, it is contrary to the trade deal. Yes, I have sent a note of diplomatic protest to the United States"? Why did he not treat this issue fair and square yesterday in the House of Commons?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just explained the position with reference to the situation. I have outlined the facts. The Hon. Leader of the Opposition never deals in facts.
He says: "What's the problem?" The problem is U.S. protectionism. We recognize the problem. Under the direction of the Prime Minister we have taken action to do something
about that. We have negotiated an agreement that will be of considerable help to Canada next year if it is implemented.
What is the solution of the Leader of the Opposition? He gets up and crabs and complains in this House, with all his Members, every day about what the Americans are doing, but he is doing nothing about it. He is going to tear up the protection that we have negotiated that will go into effect next year.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, the great protection he has negotiated does not protect our lobster fishermen, and it does not protect the potato farmers of Atlantic Canada. That is where he is.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: ALLEGED CONCESSIONS MADE TO AMERICANS-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ALLEGED CONCESSIONS MADE TO AMERICANS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why are lobster fishermen in the Gaspe, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland the victims of the trade agreement signed by the Prime Minister? Hasn't this Government made enough concessions to the United States? And why are potato producers being victimized by the trade agreement with the United States?
The Prime Minister has stated on many occasions that he would not tolerate any amendments or concessions regarding his agreement with the United States. What about these concessions on potatoes and lobster?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: ALLEGED CONCESSIONS MADE TO AMERICANS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are no concessions made to the United States at all. I just explained that the situation on potatoes is that they want to give to the President authority to negotiate, as though he needed the authority to negotiate. That is all that they are doing. There is no danger to potatoes at all.
The danger to potatoes is if the hon. gentleman were successful and got elected, which of course is not going to happen, and tears up up the agreement. Then the spuds would really be in danger. We would then have an hon. gentleman in power who said that he wished to export water, not for money but in return for access to their markets. He would exchange water and potatoes and fish for access to the Americans.

speechtext: Read the whole quote.

That is the statement of the Leader of the Opposition. We are protecting Canadians. He would sell them out just as he said he would in 1968.

May 20, 1988

subsubtopic: DROUGHT IN SOUTHERN PRAIRIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture. The drought situation in the southern prairies grows worse every day. Last weekend I had an opportunity to visit the Milk River Ridge area of southern Alberta where we saw topsoil blowing away, sloughs were dry, and dug-outs with no water in them. Still, the federal Government is not prepared to make any commitment to the farmers in that area.
I wonder if the Minister is willing to give a commitment today to provide at least the same amount of money, $28.5 million, that the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan have already committed so that they can provide emergency water systems, dug-outs, wells, and transportation systems for livestock herds.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: DROUGHT IN SOUTHERN PRAIRIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course the Government shares the Hon. Member's concern in this very serious matter. I think that he would acknowledge at the same time that there has never been a Government in the history of the country that has done as much for agriculture, and has responded to the needs of agriculture in the way in which this Government has under the leadership of the Prime Minister of Canada. The programs have been effective. We have responded generously.
I can tell the Hon. Member that the Prime Minister has instructed the Minister of Agriculture to meet with his provincial counterparts at the earliest possible date. As he knows, there has been an ongoing working group of federal and provincial officials working on this particular issue.
He should also know that there are indeed ongoing government programs to deal with this very serious problem.
He should also recognize that there is a long-term commitment, as was enunciated in the announcement in December, to the effect that we want to work very closely with the provinces in establishing a long-term soil and water conservation program that will meet all the needs of agriculture throughout Canada.

subtopic: HAY AND FEED SUPPLIES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSISTANCE
HAY AND FEED SUPPLIES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister knows that hay and feed supplies are desperately low in many of the drought areas, and that farmers are actually starting to disperse their herds, which not only cuts off their livelihoods for the next three or four years but also drives down cattle prices.
Is the Deputy Prime Minister willing to give a commitment to the farmers of western Canada today that the Government will provide emergency assistance for moving feed into those
Oral Questions
drought areas? After all, this is a national emergency that requires specific action for these livestock producers now, not vague generalities about what the Government has done in the past or may do at some time in the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: HAY AND FEED SUPPLIES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it rather strange for the Hon. Member to suggest that we deal in vague generalities when well in excess of $3 billion has been committed to western Canada this year, an increase of well over 400 per cent since the Hon. Member's Party was in office.
The fact of the matter is that there have been ongoing meetings at the officials' level. The Prime Minister has instructed the Minister of Agriculture to meet with his provincial counterparts. This is a co-ordinated effort. The provinces recognize that they have a responsibility. The federal Government has always recognized its responsibility in this regard.
I can tell the Hon. Member that this Government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, has responded to the needs of agriculture before, and will do so again.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PLYWOOD EXPORTS
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PLYWOOD EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. Earlier today in Question Period we heard questions raised about how the Government has not stood up for the interests of our lobster producers and potato producers.
My question relates to another aspect of the deal. In the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives the U.S. has proposed changes in the accord, and apparently the Government of Canada has objected.
Is the Minister aware that the wording used on the proposed change in the plywood section at the House committee level, a copy of which I have obtained today, is virtually the same as the wording used in the U.S. Senate Finance Committee, which shows that they are deadly serious about this change in the United States? By the way, it is being described in the United States as a major victory for U.S. plywood producers, allowing them greater access to the Canadian market.
Is the Minister aware that the wording is now identical at both the House and Senate levels, and that they intend to proceed with it? If the Minister is aware, has he made it clear that this further change in the deal is unacceptable to the Government of Canada, and it will not be proceeding with this deal if these changes in the wording are proceeded with in the United States?

May 20, 1988
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-PLYWOOD EXPORTS
speechtext:
Speaker, when we encounter a problem we do not throw up our hands and withdraw altogether and leave chaos in its place, as apparently the Leader of the New Democratic Party suggests. What a course of conduct that is. When one encounters a difficulty, Mr. Speaker, one continues on to overcome the difficulty.
What is happening in the United States is that the Senate Finance Committee has dealt with the markup of the proposed administration Bill as has the House Ways and Means Committee. They have to get together, have a conference, and decide what it is Congress will recommend.

With respect to the plywood situation we have pointed out to the United States that, unless it institutes the tariff cuts to which we have agreed, on January 1, it will be in violation of the Canada-U.S. FTA. If the Canada-U.S. FTA is adopted by this country, as we intend to do, and as we feel reasonably certain the United States will do, it would be in violation.
Therefore, we would have several options. One is to go to dispute settlement, because the Americans would be violating the FTA. Another option is to take our own action with respect to repositing or replying to that action by the United States, if it goes forward with it.
It has not acted yet, and we are not going to panic. We have to ask the hon. gentleman opposite what is his answer to U.S. protectionism? What are the NDP going to do? What would the hon. gentleman do if the United States gives notice that it wants to cancel the Auto Pact? What would the hon. gentleman do then? Superman Broadbent, what would his solution be?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can tell the Minister that one thing we would not do is when the Americans say "jump", unlike the Conservatives we would not say "how high?" That is the difference.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Leader of the NDP wants action. He has been wanting action now for how many years? Is it 10, 12, or 20 years? For how many years have members of the New Democratic Party been wanting action? They have been wanting it all their lives, and they are getting action. The hon. gentleman asks how high they jump. I ask the hon. gentleman is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it is Ed Broadbent hurtling over Oshawa on his way down to the United States to force the Senate and the House of Representatives to do his will.

speechtext: You are beginning to believe those polls now, are you?

speechtext:

I further point out to him that from 1982 to 1987 through the transfer payments for health and post-secondary education, the entire established programs financing portfolio, that the federal Government transferred to the provinces in the order of $65 billion. I think additionally what the Hon. Member should keep in mind is that in a number of cases provinces have not transferred the same percentage of increase they receive from the federal Government in the transfers to their institutions. If that had been done, then possibly we would not be in the dilemma we are in today.
May 20, 1988

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Justice and of the Minister of National Revenue, my question is for the Prime Minister. We have made some important advances in the last couple of years in this area, but we can do a lot more. I will inquire immediately as to the possibility of acting promptly in regard to the suggestion of my hon. friend and any other suggestions she may have in this regard.

May 20, 1988
Point of Order-Mr. Langdon INCOME TAX ACT PROVISIONS

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Prime Minister. I hope he will give personal attention to this matter.

Mr. Speaker, during Question Period today, a reference was made by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) to certain notes which have been sent to the United States with reference to sections of the Finance Committee's suggested changes to the legislation dealing with the trade agreement, and I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to Beauchesne's 1978 edition, Citation 327, which deals with documents cited and the requirements of Ministers of the Crown with respect to this. Paragraph (2) reads:
It has been admitted that a document which has been cited ought to be laid
upon the Table of the House, if it can be done without injury to the public
interest.
In view of this rule which binds us in the House of Commons, I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, if it would be possible for you to ascertain from the Minister for International Trade if there is in fact any potential or actual injury to the public interest which might exist if these protest notes to the United States were laid upon the Table. If there is no such injury to our national interest, I would ask that these documents be in fact laid upon the Table further to that rule.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I can help other Hon. Members who might wish to contribute to this question by pointing out that we had this matter before us only a little while ago, and a question of whether or not a Minister is quoting from a document becomes of some considerable concern to the Chair.
If the Member is quoting from a document, the rule is clearly as the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) states it to be. If it is something less than a quote, it puts the Chair in some difficulty, and I ask Hon. Members to address that point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the precedents on this matter speak not only of quotations but also
May 20, 1988

of citing documents. I respectfully submit there must be some distinction between the meaning of the word "quote" and the meaning of the word "cite". Otherwise, the precedents in question would not have covered both those words in setting out a basis for requiring Ministers to table documents they refer to in debate or in answering questions. Therefore, I know you will want to review the "blues" to see exactly in what way and in what context the Minister referred to the notes in question.
I submit that the precedents are clear. It is not necessary for the Minister to quote at length or in any substantial fashion from the documents in question. It is sufficient that he cite them, and I repeat that there must be some difference in meaning between the words "quote" and "cite", otherwise the precedents would not have made reference to both those words in setting out conditions for the requirement that documents referred to by Ministers in this House have to be tabled once they are referred to.
I also want to point out that the Minister, at no time in the answers he gave, made any suggestion or gave any hint that there be anything contrary to national security or the public interest in making their contents public. On the contrary, he took great delight in referring to those notes and their existence as supporting the position of the Government that it was in fact doing what it should in defence of the best interests of this country.
I ask you to take into account the context in which the Minister made reference to the notes. I would think that he would be delighted, if not to table the notes forthwith in the House, to release them publicly as soon as possible today. I certainly think it would be consistent with the Minister's responsibility to this House to disclose those notes first by tabling them here, and he has time to do that up until three o'clock. However, if there is some problem in getting the text of the notes in both official languages before three o'clock in such a way that they can be made public, then he need not, and in fact should not, wait until next Tuesday. He should make them public as a press release as soon as possible later today.
To conclude, I say the precedents are clear. The context in which the Minister made reference to the notes is also clear. He has a definite obligation to table the notes in question in their complete form forthwith. Anything else would be not only contrary to the precedents in question, it would be a failure to show the respect which any Member, especially a Minister, owes to this House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I want to thank the Hon. Member for his intervention. He points out an important addition to the argument and also a distinction. I have taken the point that he raises and I will keep it in mind.
