subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted by Question Period, I had been pointing out that in addition to the debt problem faced by the poorest countries in the world, there is a decline in official development assistance, and then I went on to talk about the most serious problem, and that is, the decline in commodity prices. I was reading from Roy Culpeper's study "Forced Adjustment: The Export Collapse in Sub-Saharan Africa" in which he states:
No commodity category was exempt: food, non-food, agricultural and mineral commodities alike plunged to their lowest level, in real terms, since the Great Depression half a century ago.
Other World Bank estimates provide forecasts of commodity prices over the next 15 years, under various assumptions about global supply and demand conditions and the economic environment. These projections indicate that the price deterioration which has occurred during 1980-86 is expected to continue in 1987 before commodity prices rise again.
However, prices are not expected to rise much in coming years, with the result that by the year 2000, they will still be lower in real terms than the depressed levels of 1985. By the turn of the century, real commodity prices, according to this scenario, will only be one-half their 1950 levels!
This is the problem facing African nations and other poor nations around the world which depend for their export earnings on commodity prices. They have declined drastically. They will continue to decline in real prices.
In fact, it has been estimated that in 1986 there was a net outflow of funds from Africa amounting to some $16 billion American. That is made up by the fact that funds coming into Africa were some $16 billion of development assistance from all countries. There was private lending amounting to only some $2 billion. This amounts to a total of $18 billion going into Africa. Going out of Africa there was a drop in commodity prices of $19 billion. Debt servicing amounted to some $15 billion. This amounts to a total of $34 billion.
This is why our Ambassador to the United Nations, Stephen Lewis, a person who has spent a great deal of time in the last three or four years visiting Africa studying the situation there and working with the United Nations trying to get a program of action that will actually meet the problems of Africa has

May 20, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
said time and time again that the West is betraying the African continent.
Perhaps we could look at the words of a distinguished African President, President Kaunda, who is the head of the Organization of African Unity. On October 6 he spoke before the United Nations General Assembly. He said that:
-almost one and a half years after the adoption of the Program, and despite some limited initiatives here and there, the international community's over-all response has fallen far short of the requirements of the Program. The international community has not lived up to its side of the recovery pact.. .
Africa has been losing on all counts ... No measures are in sight to stabilize export earnings from commodities, which are of major interest to Africa; nor have effective mechanisms been put in place to deal with the unmanageable debt and debt-servicing burdens in any meaningful way. Worse still, the anticipated increase in the resource flows to Africa has not materialized. Not only have they not matched the resource outflows from Africa, they have actually stagnated.
He concluded by stating that:
-unless effective solutions are found for the debt and commodity problems and unless resource flows at levels adequate to compensate for the outward transfer of resources away from Africa are ensured, prospects for bringing about recovery and development in Africa will become forever elusive and the continent will forever be a victim of the vagaries and misery of perpetual crisis.
This is the problem about which we are concerned. The fund that we are talking about contributing to will establish approximately $6 billion in special drawing rights, a little over $10 billion Canadian, or a little over $8 billion American. Yet that is going to be spent over a number of years to help with the debt problem. We are talking about a situation in Africa alone where there is a net shortfall of $16 billion per year. Thus the enhanced structural adjustment facility, ESAF, is not going to meet the total needs of the African continent. We should not be under any illusion that it will do that. It is a small step. It is a step that is primarily designed to ensure that the poorest countries do not default to their creditors in the West or to the IMF itself.
In our Party we are concerned that Canada should be doing more for Africa. We are concerned that when Canada meets with the other leaders of the industrialized West at the G-7 meeting in Toronto next month we should be pushing for more human adjustment policies on the part of the IMF. We should be pushing for a greater role by the World Bank and its concessionary flows to the poorest countries. We should be putting some pressure on the United States because, inadequate as ESAF is, the United States has said it will not be contributing anything to it.
Here we are talking about a trade arrangement with the United States. We want to get in under its protectionist umbrella, so-called. We are not going to quite make it. We will be standing with quite a bit of our shoulders and our head outside the umbrella with it dripping down on us. However, we want to get in under the American umbrella. Yet the United States is pleading poor. It says it cannot make any contributions to this enhanced structural adjustment facility that is supposed to be helping the poorest nations in the world. It says that it is too poor itself.
This raises questions as to why we are getting involved in a trade arrangement with another nation that is not able to carry its weight in international terms. It is able to throw its weight around on the International Monetary Fund but it is not able to carry its weight in terms of helping the poor nations.
We would like to see Canada take a more straightforward position on this matter and work with other nations to ensure that multilateral agencies such as the IMF and the World Bank have better structural policies that take account of the impact of those policies upon the poorest of the poor. We want to see Canada take a better position in terms of itself increasing the amount of official development assistance that goes to the poorest of the poor.
I remind the House and I remind the Canadian people of the commitment that was made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he appeared before the United Nations shortly after the Conservative Government was elected. He said that Canada would reach its commitment to guarantee 0.7 per cent of its Gross National Product to official development assistance by 1990. That is a commitment that Canada made. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made that commitment in our name to the poor peoples of the world. It is a commitment that the Government has welched on. I regret that as a Canadian who would like to see us living up to our commitments. We should be taking action.
We must place back on the agenda the need for a new international economic order. We have to be working for some system that will stabilize world commodity prices. It is in our interests as well as in the interests of the poorest nations in the world that their economies should not be allowed to collapse because of the way in which commodity prices have collapsed.
Thus we have this agenda. It is a big agenda. We support the small step that the establishment of the enhanced structural adjustment facility makes. But we want to emphasize that there are other items that need to be addressed also if we are going to take at all a comprehensive approach to Africa and not be simply a drop in the bucket.
Finally, I want to reiterate that we want to see this Bill tightened up in terms of not giving a blank cheque to the Government so that it can simply increase the money, at any time it wants and so that it can give money to any fund that it wants without coming back to Parliament. We believe it is extremely important that Parliament should continue to have control over the purse, that when we are talking about such matters as contributions to the International Monetary Fund the Government should be accountable to the House of Commons for the way in which the IMF operates. If we are giving money to it, if we are providing Canadian taxpayers' money then we should insist that the Government be accountable for the way in which the IMF spends that money.

subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have a chance to speak on Bill C-126 because it raises a very serious problem. That is to say, on the one hand it undertakes
May 20, 1988

to give aid to the needy. It asks those countries that have money to provide money to lend to those that lack it. On the other hand, our experience over several years now with this kind of lending process is not encouraging because it seems that the results that we were going to get are just not there.
Furthermore, I believe that this Bill takes a direction which is unwise and unfortunate in that it removes from the House almost all effective responsibility and oversight for future contributions to the International Monetary Fund. Bill C-126, an Act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act, has two short clauses. The first states, in part:
"5.1(1) The Minister of Finance may lend to the International Monetary Fund, at such rate of interest and on such other terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve, such sum or sums of money as may be required for funding any trust or body established by the Fund ...
In other words, it will not only go to specified purposes now existing in the fund, but if new purposes and new programs are created, they need not be discussed, and probably will not be discussed in the House of Commons, because the Minister now has the power to direct it anywhere he or the IMF please.
The Minister can direct it "as may be required for funding any trust or body established by the Fund to assist in fulfilling the purposes of the fund ..." Those are very broadly stated purposes, which the fund does not necessarily carry out, such as maintaining the income level of the people in the country to which it lends.
That clause further states, "not exceeding in the whole five hundred and fifty million dollars, or such greater amount as may be fixed by the Governor in Council". If the Governor in Council decides to put in a further $1 billion or $10 billion, he or she does not need to return to Parliament to ask for the money. We have now said it may be any amount that the Governor in Council thinks would be reasonable.
The second clause states that, "the Minister of Finance may grant..." The first clause states "lend" and the second clause states:
... grant to the International Monetary Fund, on such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve, such sum or sums of money as may be required for funding any trust or body established by the Fund to assist in fulfilling the purposes of the Fund, not exceeding in the whole two hundred and fifty million dollars, or such greater amount as may be fixed by the Governor in Council.
In other words, this Bill gives the Cabinet a blank cheque in its lending or granting to the International Monetary Fund. It is a blank cheque not only in the limits to which it can grant or lend, but also in the purposes and the bodies to which it can grant or lend. If the International Monetary Fund had a really good record of helping the people it is supposed to help, that would be more acceptable. But it does not.
I wish to move from the dry figures and dry legal words to what I saw a couple of years ago when I was on parliamentary business in Guatemala. I wish to speak about the man with the hoe. There is a famous portrait that was produced in Europe of
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
a man with a hoe. This is a different man with a different hoe. In the famous European picture the man with the hoe has a hoe similar to that which we would use in our gardens. The hoe being used by the man in Guatemala was at least twice or perhaps four times as large, a really heavy tool. As we drove past this person in the countryside, I was told by the officials that that was the only technological improvement brought to the indigenous peoples of Central America by five centuries of European conquest and occupation.
This man with the hoe was brother or cousin to the others whom I saw there. They were lifting their hoes to dig at a hillside which was at least 45 degrees steep, and sometimes 60 degrees steep. That was the only land that they could work, the only land that they were allowed to have. On the road I saw one of his brothers or cousins carrying a load of firewood, logs that had been split and sawed. It was a huge load about the size that he was himself. He was carrying this load of firewood from where it could be cut to where he would need it for his family. Behind him was a woman carrying on her head a large bundle of sticks, also for firewood.
It was explained to me by our CIDA officials that the gathering of Firewood for cooking and the gathering of water for cooking on those mountainous hills occupy several hours a day of a peasant's time. No wonder these people are poor. For a few days or weeks in a year they may go down to the coastlands for a day labour at low rates for the cotton harvest, the sugar harvest, or similar work. But all in all, 80 per cent of their children are suffering malnutrition. I believe it is obvious that that is not a condition that has gone on for many centuries. The fact that 80 per cent of the children of a country are suffering malnutrition is a modern invention.
The man with the hoe is contributing a small amount, but he is contributing to the wealth of Canada, the United States, and the other banker countries. It was pointed out by my colleague that the people of the Third World, of which this country is a part, last year contributed almost $6 billion in outflow, that is, $6 billion more went out than came in. That is $6 billion from the poorest to the richest. That is why I think of the man with the hoe when I look at this Bill.
There is another reason why I think of the man with the hoe. When I grew up in Winnipeg during the Depression I heard that there were two kinds of farmers: there were those farmers who farm the land, and there were those who farm the farmers. That farming of the farmers has not stopped in Canada, but it has been powerfully extended to Guatemala and dozens of other countries of the former colonies of Europe that we now call the Third World. They are exporting food from Guatemala because there is plenty of rich land. Guatemala is not the Sahara Desert, or even the Sahel. Guatemala has some of the richest farm land one could find, with an excellent climate and fertile soil on the flat bottom land.
Generations ago the landowners and the military drove the indigenous people, who are the great majority in the country,

May 20, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
off the good land into the hills. They did not kill all of them because they were needed for cheap labour. As I said, come harvest time for a few days or weeks they are needed to work for a pittance down near the coast. There they are on the hills, unable to feed their children properly, but supposed to survive as a pool of surplus labour, the reserve army of the unemployed.
Whether it is through the IMF, the IAB, or any of the other multiple lending sources, those organizations lend money to countries such as Guatemala, El Salvador, or to many other countries in the same condition. These loans are mainly contributed by the countries of Europe and America, and mainly used to police countries of the Third World to ensure that they will structure their economy in such a way as to enable them to repay not only the IMF, but also their loans from the private banks.
It happens that in Central America three-quarters of the $17 billion debt, which has been created mainly in the last eight years, because it was $7 billion in 1980, is owed to Governments, that is, bilateral debts, or to multilateral institutions such as the IMF. This does not include the $600 million that is provided annually by the United States for the military. It is clear why the military are needed. They are needed in order to stop the rebellion of people who do not like supporting the IMF and the other creditors in the style to which we have become accustomed. In fact, of the 25 million people in Central America, every man, woman, and child is charged by us with owing us $700. People who do not see $100 in a year are supposed to owe us $700. People in lands where we have taken out gold, silver, timber, cotton, sugar, bananas, coffee and all kinds of mineral and agricultural wealth, are now considered by our laws to be debtors to us. Every man, woman and child, including those suffering malnutrition, on average in Central America, is charged with owing us $700. It is bizarre. It is obscene.
The only way that they can pay it, of course, by our standards, is by producing their cheap labour to keep the price of our coffee, our sugar, our cotton, our bananas, carnations and other beautiful flowers and so on, low enough so that we will be able to afford them easily and never come within sight of the kind of malnutrition that their children suffer.
The role of the IMF is illustrated in this Bill but not in full detail. The information from the departmental staff indicates that loans will be made at 0.5 per cent to certain countries under conditions that they tighten the screws still further on their population in order to repay. But the grant will be used to make up the difference between that one-half per cent and whatever is the rate, perhaps 8 per cent, 10 per cent or 12 per cent, at which the IMF will receive the money from the creditor countries. In other words, the borrowers-the people in countries like Africa and Central America, Latin America-are not really benefiting by this so-called easy or cheap interest rate. It is the Fund itself which benefits and, along
with that, about 13.5 per cent of the repayments go to the private banks. The private banks in our country benefit by the kind of money that is being put in as proposed in this Bill today.
The responsibility for repaying the loan is attributed to countries like Guatemala, El Salvador, Brazil, Peru and so on, but the benefit of it does not come to them. On paper there is a benefit. Instead of being in debt for 50 years, they will be allowed to pay it more slowly and be in debt for 100 years to come. In other words, they will be locked into what is called debt peonage.
The basis of this debt peonage is the declining prices of agricultural and other raw products, but primarily agricultural products.
At a conference yesterday dealing with Central America, we were told by an official of CIDA that there is no use trying to stop the decline of agricultural prices. That is a very convenient statement of fact. Is it not nice for us coffee drinkers that it is impossible to stop the lowering of the price of coffee to the men and women who actually produce it? I suppose, according to our officials, it is supposed to be some inevitable law of God that agricultural prices must decline and there is nothing we can do about it, so we say. Certainly there is nothing we can do about it by the rules we have created.
I think the principal thought for the IMF under these circumstances was actually enunciated a century ago by Lewis Carroll in Alice in Wonderland and the verses about the walrus and the carpenter.
After they invited the oysters for a walk and were eating them, the oysters complained. The verse is:
"I weep for you", the walrus said; I deeply sympathize, with sobs and tears he sorted out those of the largest size, holding his pocket handkerchief before his streaming eyes.
The carpenter was complaining that the walrus only held the handkerchief in front of his eyes so that the carpenter could not see how many oysters he was eating.
Lewis Carroll thought he was joking, but apparently the IMF has taken him seriously. What we heard yesterday at the round table conference on Central America, for example, concerns this same point, the prices of agricultural products.
Mr. Gabriel Siris, Director of the country program of the Economic Committee for the Latin American countries of the United Nations, told us in part that;
Another determinant of today's economic crisis is the downturn in exports of traditional goods, which in the past had been the principal engine of growth for these economies.
He is referring to Central America.
He went on to say:
Basic agriculture commodities, such as coffee, cotton, and bananas constitute a major source of savings for investment in other sectors, principally industry.
May 20, 1988

He went on to detail the sharp drop in world prices of their chief export commodities. For the seven years from 1980 to 1987, coffee dropped 41 per cent; cotton dropped 31 per cent; bananas dropped 7 per cent; sugar dropped 83 per cent; and beef dropped 12 per cent. With such a sharp drop, he said that it is no accident that every country in the region has slid into economic depression during this decade, regardless of its degree of civil strife or the prevailing political structure. He went on to say:
Preliminary estimates indicate that the losses resulting from decreases in the
volume of traditional export goods average more than half a billion dollars a
year; the losses attributable to drops in prices are even greater.
Therefore, more than half a billion dollars is taken out of those countries by the devices that our countries use to force agricultural prices down.
I do not see any sign that the IMF will change its policy. We read in the newspapers that it will not. An article yesterday in the Ottawa Citizen quotes Mr. Camdessus as saying: "I see no readiness by Governments of the major creditor countries to entertain such an approach."
He was referring to debt relief. He refers also to the desperate condition not just of Central America but to the whole of Latin America.
The same principle applies in Latin America as in Central America, as in Africa. The IMF is not helping those countries to recover. It is driving them deeper into the hole. Unless Canada can persuade the IMF, along with other countries, to alter its policy then the money we put in there does not help them but hurts them. It only benefits the banks in our countries.

speechtext:
My colleague said that it almost comes down to the man with the hoe. I agree with him, except that to a large extent in the world today it comes down to the woman with the hoe or even the child with the hoe.
The reality is that entire families are forced into wage slavery, producing these commodities where the bottom has dropped out of prices.
I am reminded of the old story of the company store. The harder you work, the more you owe. You owe your soul to the company store. We have had ample illustration of that in some of the single industry towns in Canada, Mr. Speaker, where people were literally locked into a kind of wage slavery. The company store would extend credit to them. When it looked as though people might be going under, the company store would extend a little more credit to them, always keeping them on the hook. In a sense that is what the IMF has done.
The Member spoke about this vicious spiral that we have. It is a downward spiral. It is not just a vicious cycle. It is a vicious downward spiral with a drop in commodity prices. That in turn leads the poor people of the poor countries to produce more to try to make up the short-fall for the drop in prices.
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
When they produce more there is a glut in the market, causing a further decline in commodity prices. This vicious downward spiral has a direct impact upon the poor.
How can this vicious cycle be broken? What steps should Canada be taking? What steps should the IMF be taking? What steps would the Members, like the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to take next month when he meets with the other so-called world leaders in Toronto?

subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext:
I thank my hon. colleague for his question, Mr. Speaker. I recognize that he has a strong background on this subject through his work in connection with official development aid through CIDA.
The question that he poses is one which I think should be addressed by a committee when this Bill, after second reading, is referred to committee. I would hope this very question would receive very close attention in the committee. Although I may not be a member of it, I would be interested if possible in attending and assisting in the work of that committee.
As to what could be done, I believe the answer has to be that the kind of conditionality traditionally imposed by the International Monetary Fund must be changed. Instead of conditions forcing countries to export more and therefore often to import more machinery, fuel, herbicides, fertilizer and so on, the conditions to be required by the IMF should rather concern the well-being of the people of a particular country, not the well-being of the IMF. Is the IMF following policies which enable people to eat better, to have schools for their children and to have decent houses? That is not expected all in one year, but is the IMF moving in that direction? If not, the IMF should seek ways in which it can move in that direction and not look at the balance of exports and the ability to repay debts.
A proposal was put forward by a number of people at a conference held in Oxford last month at which a Member from each Party in Canada attended. The debt repayments from Central America mostly owed to governments and multilateral groups should be retained in Central America in the Central American Bank and recycled for the development of Central America, particularly for projects that would encourage two or more countries to co-operate together.
A suggestion was made that a railroad could be built running the length of Central America, a revolutionary proposal, Mr. Speaker. There are railroads but there is no Central American railroad, only feeder lines running down to the sea. A railroad might help to bring those people together and avoid future wars. Mr. Speaker, when this Bill came before us, I looked at it and it looked entirely innocuous. Had it been brought forward quickly, there might have been no debate on it at all. That is really too bad, and it says something about deficiencies in our process.
This Bill, which is an Act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act, is in fact of major importance. It provides the House an opportunity to discuss the debt crisis in the Third World, and of course, that is one of those issues which is important and in fact absolutely crucial to the future of our world but which this particular Parliament seldom if ever discusses.
When members of the public complain that we are a bit trivial and are worried only about what Minister is taking loans from whom or how many pairs of shoes so and so happens to keep in his closet or something like that, and why do we not talk about the important things, I would reply that today we have such an opportunity and I would hope that Members of the Progressive Conservative and Liberal Parties in the House of Commons would take the opportunity to discuss this very serious question.
Let us make no mistake. We are talking about some 120 less developed countries. Their debt now amounts to about one and one-quarter trillion dollars. A lot of that debt was run up during the 1970s during the oil crisis when there was a great deal of recycling of oil revenues which went through the banks of the developed, industrialized world and were then put into the less developed countries.

May 20, 1988

Unfortunately, for political or other reasons many of those loans have not proven to be particularly good. In particular, the ability of those countries to support that debt, to use it for development and to pay it off has been tragically undermined because of the change in relative commodity prices over the course of the last eight or ten years and because of the recession in the industrial world at the beginning of the 1980s. As well, it is because, dare I say it, of the fact that the major markets for goods, services and commodities that could be sold by the developing world, the markets in the industrial countries, have not been particularly receptive to the kind of growth those countries would have needed in order to maintain the debt that was almost forced upon them back in the late 1970s at the time of the oil crisis.
As my colleague from Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands has already indicated, the New Democratic Party is glad that this issue is being debated in the House of Commons through Bill C-126, and we are taking this debate very seriously. At the same time, we are uneasy about this Bill. It indicates the kind of priority the Government has given to the Bill. When the Government of Canada proposes to play its part in a $10 billion facility to help the poorest of the less developed countries, it does so in the form of a two page Bill which gives almost no clue in the explanatory notes as to what it is all about. I do not think that this subject deserves such paltry treatment as that.
This Bill provides for Canada to advance about $550 million Canadian, equivalent to about 300 million special drawing right units or SDR units of the IMF, to the International Monetary Fund for its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, plus an additional $250 million in grants to the same facility.
This Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility was agreed to at the Venice Summit meeting of the seven economic powers in June of 1987 and calls for a total enhancement of about $10 billion Canadian or 6 billion SDRs to provide funding to deal with the structural development programs of the poorest developing countries. There was already a facility in place that was begun in 1986. This is also known as a structural adjustment facility, and it had a value of 2.7 billion SDRs.
The idea is that the money in the fund will be lent at very low interest rates of one-half of 1 per cent by the IMF to the poorest countries in order to allow them to service debts and to maintain necessary imports. The difference between that and market interest rates will be made up by grants from the participating countries such as Canada.
As far as Canada is concerned, to some extent, we are committing foreign aid funds into the 1990s. The $250 million in grants for this facility will be used up in a few years, and we will be looking at a continuing commitment for this interest rate subsidy of perhaps $50 million a year as long as this Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility stays in place.
As my colleague has already pointed out, this particular provision is a double-edged sword for the very poor countries.
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
Advances from the International Monetary Fund will be accompanied by policy advice from the IMF relative to economic growth, deficits, export-oriented policies and privatization policies pursued by the developing countries in question. This means that this facility is a means for the western industrial nations to impose their agendas on developing countries. I will return to that in a few moments, because it seems to me that that is very important and could be and is very dangerous.
Let us look at the price the developed countries are paying in order to impose their agendas on large numbers of developing countries. It is not that great when one considers that the current total of Third World debt is about a trillion and a quarter dollars or $1,250 billion or thereabouts, and $10 billion in this enhanced structural adjustment facility is therefore less than 1 per cent of the outstanding amount of the debt. However, many of the less developed countries are so poor, so desperate, that they have no choice but to accept the money from the International Monetary Fund and the advice that goes with it. It seems to me that that is a matter about which we should express some very real concern.
My friend and colleague, a former NDP Member from Saskatoon, Father Bob Ogle, went with a Parliamentary Committee to Brazil a few years ago, and I met him when he came back. I asked him what he found, and he told me that he had been able, through his networks, because he served as a missionary in northern Brazil, to see people and to go places to which the committee would not have been taken by the Brazilian Government or even by our own diplomats because they do not know the areas that well.
He remarked that when he went to towns where he had worked 10 or 15 years earlier as a missionary, he went to the markets and saw what the people there were carrying home from the markets. I recall the conversation I had with him very vividly. He said: "If you are living at that level of development, then everything you can spend on food, you spend, so that when you go to the market and take your week's food home, you are taking everything you can afford. You have paid whatever else you have to pay in terms of rent or any taxes or other things you have to pay", and he said what people were taking home to their families in the early 1980s was only just over half of what they had been taking home 10 or 15 years earlier.
To me and to Father Ogle, that was a vivid example of just what is happening in that part of Brazil, a country which has substantial industrial development in the southern industrial area between Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.
At a recent convention my Party took on this question of the agenda the IMF has been imposing upon the Third World. My Party does not always refer to its convention resolutions in the House of Commons, but this time I think it is particularly apt and deserves quoting. Policy (b)3(2) says in part that the IMF,

in pursuit of monetarist objectives, has imposed conditions upon Third World countries which have led to drastic devaluations of currencies, reduction of already low wage levels, elimination of food subsidies, and cut-backs in social services. Enforcement of these unpopular policies has required repressive internal security measures which are directly counter to development. At that point we, assembled in our convention, called upon the Government of Canada to respond positively to Third World proposals for immediate debt relief such as the repayment at a rate equal to a ceiling of 10 per cent of export earnings proposed by the President of Peru, Alan Garcia Perez.
That was the proposal, but the situation we have now is such that it is estimated in the last five or six years there has been some $125 billion more sucked out of poor, less-developed countries in debt servicing and debt repayment than went into those countries. Those countries have perforce followed the script written by the IMF and the industrial countries in a way which I do not believe would be tolerable in this country.
Recently the Canada-Mexico parliamentary group met here. We talked at length about Third World debt. The people we talked to were representatives of the Popular Revolution Party, the governing Party for the last 50 or 60 years in Mexico, a country with an unusual form of democracy. The message they brought to us was that there have to be answers. The problems of debt servicing are killing Mexico, a country which is rather more advanced with a higher per capita income and higher standard of industrial development than many of the other less-developed countries.
During the period of office of the current President of Mexico, real wages for Mexican workers have tumbled by 30 per cent, 40 per cent or 50 per cent. The level of underemployment and unemployment is tragic. Even in the industrialized areas immediately adjacent to the U.S. border, workers are paid the equivalent of about 40 cents or 50 cents an hour Canadian. That is a good wage compared to the standard in the rest of Mexico.
When I got home last night I noticed an article in The Ottawa Citizen from The New York Times Service which talked about concern throughout Latin America, which was reflected when I met with the Mexican parliamentarians just a few weeks ago. A number of people, including economists from different Latin American countries, point out that over the past five years alone Latin America has financed $145 billion in debt repayment. What they are saying is that the IMF prescriptions have now been tested in 28 of the 32 Latin American and Caribbean nations, the policy of what is called investment through growth. That policy has produced adjustments but it has not produced growth. It has not produced an ability to solve the problems of those particular people. In fact, it has produced exactly the contrary.
I will give another example which would perhaps indicate the depth of the problem. The other day I was speaking to someone from Jamaica. There, because of import duties and
conditions of life and that kind of thing, an ordinary man's shirt can cost $50 or $60. A Datsun automobile which might sell second-hand for $3,000 or $4,000 in this country costs $30,000 or $40,000. Of course, incomes are far lower there than here. That gives you an idea of the disparities that exist there.
The IMF, according to the Latin Americans, has four commandments: Get your prices right; balance your budget; open up the economy; and privatize. All at the same time. I would like to ask my colleague from Thunder Bay-Nipigon, or my colleague from Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands, or my colleague from Spadina, all NDP Members, where they have heard that particular prescription before. I know where we have heard it. We have heard it from Washington and Ronald Reagan. We have heard it from the United Kingdom and Margaret Thatcher. We have heard it from the Fraser Institute. We have heard it from all the gurus of the right in the U.S. and the U.K.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in this very important debate on Bill C-126. As my colleagues have already pointed out, this debate gives us a very important opportunity to consider the profound problems which have arisen in the developing countries in these last years, problems which began to develop in the 1970s and have during this decade reached tragic dimensions for country after country.
We here in Canada, whether Members of Parliament or so many of our citizens are often insulated from the situation that exists. However, I recognize in my own constituency of Thunder Bay-Nipigon some of the smaller communities, particularly those which are Indian reserves, about which the Canadian Government has done so little, that the Canadian people have failed so badly to recognize the challenges of development. There certainly are areas in Canada of misery. However, what has happened in one country after another of the so-called Third World during these last years is a tragic situation which the proposal of the Government has put before us will do little to resolve. In fact, one might say it will do nothing to resolve it. It may go some little way toward helping. But there is not here in these proposals any kind of a resolution.
After all, the Bill proposes to authorize contributions by Canada to an enhanced structural adjustment facility which will be operated within the International Monetary Fund-World Bank arrangements which date back to the Bretton Woods Conference of 1944. This facility, this pooling of a certain amount of western, industrial financial resources, to make available in the way of concessionary financing at very low interest rates to countries is on the right track. When it is such a limited facility, when it adds to the 2.7 billion in the way of special drawing right units that was put into an earlier facility in 1986, another 6 billion of these SDR units, an addition of some $10 billion, we have only very limited action when we recognize that the debt of the developing countries in fact exceeds $1 trillion U.S. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), has pointed out that it is $1.25 trillion of debt.
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
We in the Democratic caucus are profoundly concerned about the inadequacy of the arrangement. We are perhaps even more profoundly concerned about the failure of the G-7, the leaders of the industrial countries, including of course the Canadian Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who in June of 1987 at the summit in Venice agreed to deal with the situation that faces us.
1 am particularly concerned about the situation because of what has happened in sub-Saharan Africa and perhaps across the whole continent of Africa. We have among us of course people with various interests. My friend, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), has a profound concern about the Central American and Latin American situation. I had the enormous privilege as an undergraduate student 25 years ago last summer of spending the summer of 1962 in West Africa as an Operations Crossroads Africa participant in a student group of largely American students, with one Mexican student. I was the Canadian in the group as it happened.
The dozen of us spent a month in a work camp in northern Ghana. We spent additional time visiting other parts of Ghana. We also spent a few days in Nigeria as well. I will never forget those experiences, which were among the most formative of my life, in sharpening my perception of the lives and the history of various peoples. It was an enormously exciting time to be in West Africa. Those were the days of independence. The Black Star stood proudly on the tower in Accra and President Kwame Nkrumah anticipated independence in country after country in black Africa. There was such enormous hope about what independence would enable the African peoples to achieve. There was even then some recognition of the economic ties that these countries were still living within. Economic neo-colonialism was certainly one of the concerns expressed in those days. However, there was all the excitement about development in Africa 25 years ago.
We would gather at public events, hold hands in a circle and sing John Donne's No Man is an Island. There in the reminder of the unity that a Canadian later on put in the language of the global village was something of the personal experience sharing with Africans in their hopes. John Donne reminds us: "-and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee". I ask this afternoon in debating this particular proposal whether among us there is much recognition of the fact that the poverty, the distress, the disease, the degradation, the death of thousands, of hundreds of thousands-millions in the cumulative sense-of people around the globe in these various countries, recognition among us that the bell is tolling and that it has its terrible overtones and consequences for us if we fail to recognize that reality.
These countries which looked forward to a great future of development have ended up falling into what can simply be described as debt slavery. The Hon. Member for Spadina spoke of debt peonage which puts it into the language of Central America. Here are whole countries ground down into

May 20, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
slavery under the demands of the western nations, the commercial banks, and that financial structure created at the end of the Second World War in order to bring prosperity to the world. That debt poverty and slavery that grips and grinds down so many of the people of this earth is the final commentary on the failure of the arrangements made in the mid-1940s.
The leaders of the industrial countries are maintaining the demands of the International Monetary Fund that the obligations incurred in the 1970s and the 1980s are met. There has been some forgiveness. The current Government deserves some credit for the forgiveness to the seven poorest African countries. In a large measure there is still the requirement that the payments be made. The payments can only be made if the countries have a balance in their trade in order that they can earn the foreign exchange required to make the payments. Consequently, exports have to be pushed and imports have to be cut back, and there should be a balance available in such circumstances. To some extent a government could decide to follow that course. In the Nkrumah days that Government did limit imports in order to ensure that foreign exchange was available for development purposes. That is not happening these days. That money leaves Africa, or the countries of Latin America, or the Asian countries, in order to meet obligations incurred in the 1970s.
Without spending any amount of time on how that happened, in facing up to the responsibility we have here, we ought to recognize that when the price of petroleum was driven up by OPEC in the early 1970s and the whole western financial system got busy with what it could do with all this money, which could not be digested or absorbed by the OPEC countries, it ended up as deposits in the western banks. Deposits are liabilities. What is wanted are assets, and assets are loans. Banks internationally, as they did in Canada in those years, were pushing loans to build up their assets in a wild rush to destruction. Now the leaders of the industrialized countries, the International Monetary Fund directors, and the World Bank are involved in trying to head off that destruction that follows from that type of activity.
Given our complicity, that of the leaders of the industrialized countries, and the leaders of financial institutions, and what happened in the 1970s and 1980s, surely in the circumstances of loans that were made that could not be repaid in any sensible manner, and loans that were not oriented to development which would not achieve the type of profits required to pay off the debt incurred, it is necessary to take up the need for action.
I will not take the time to indicate in detail how tragic the situation has become in Africa. When we recognize that the debt service has now reached the level of 50 per cent of Gross National Product, one recognizes the type of shackles on African countries. When one contemplates the fact that the level of per capita income fell between 1980 and 1986 by 10.8 per cent, this is the very opposite of development.
For many years, one of the most impressive countries in western Africa was the Ivory Coast. It has been quite impressive in using western financial resource connections with France, particularly to develop itself. From statistics of per capita income, in the 1980s the per capita income in that country has fallen by no less than 23 per cent. That is the personal experience of individuals in those countries in the debt slavery imposed upon them.
Does Canada have a responsibility? Surely the answer can only be yes. Does Canada have the possibility of doing something about it? I would suggest if we return to the origins of Bretton Woods, some Members may wish to look at A.F.W. Plumptre's account of the organization of the Bretton Woods system. At the time Canada played its part between the Americans and the British. John Maynard Keynes was the British negotiator who was pressing for international arrangements that would make it possible for Britain to continue after the war and to continue after the U.S. lend-lease credits were cut off so abruptly when the war ended in Europe. He hoped for the type of assistance for reconstruction that was required, and he did not get it. Canada did all that it could to assist in that. In fact, in terms of lending to Britain in 1946 and 1947, Canada did more than the U.S. by a large measure, in fact to such an extent that Canada ended up in financial difficulties in 1947, which were only resolved by a combination of Canada's getting a share in the Marshall Plan expenditures by the U.S. and developments in the petroleum industry.
The fact is that in 1947 the United States recognized responsibilities for Europe that it had not seen when it was negotiating the International Monetary Fund arrangements in 1944 and 1945. The U.S. recognized the necessity of the Marshall Plan arrangements for European reconstruction. That recognition seems to point the way to what is required now. Canadian recognition of what is needed, and Canadian pressure on the United States to change its policies to recognize, as my colleagues have been pointing out, that orientation to the market, privatization, the imposition of these economic policies that I have been denouncing on one country after another lead not to development, but a grinding down into abject poverty for those countries.
There are proposals on the table that have been put forward as against the proposals of Mr. Baker from the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury which are very limited and piecemeal. What is required is to start with the most fundamental truth for the industrialized countries. If these countries of the Third World around the globe are forced to put all their resources and all their foreign exchange earnings into keeping the western banking structure going, we will end up in depression. As the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) pointed out, the U.S. decline as an exporter through this decade has been based on the fact that if a country cannot export what will happen to its industry?
The first principle and understanding is to recognize that somehow or another we need to take the weight of the western financial system off those countries for our own survival and in
May 20, 1988

order to ensure that we are able to export, and do not see all the earnings of those countries ending up simply propping up the world banking structure.
I will end my comments at this point for lack of time. It is that type of wisdom that we have not seen from the Government which is so desperately needed for our sake and for the sake of the people of the entire earth.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext: It being two o'clock, the House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business.
[ Translation]

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a special salary insurance protection fund or corporation, responsible for ensuring that workers will get salaries owed to them at the time when the Canadian enterprise where they are employed has declared bankruptcy.
-He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for this opportunity to present a motion that has been postponed several times, for various reasons, especially since Friday is not a day generally used to discuss Private Members' Business.
Mr. Speaker, I may add that after my motion was put on the Order Paper, there was a great deal of consultation, and the Government reacted favourably, since the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) said in the House this week that he expected to be able to introduce a bill, before the end of the next session, of course.
I would now like to explain my reasons for presenting this motion. First of all, corporate bankruptcies in Canada come under the Bankruptcy Act. This legislation, which came into effect in 1949, is now completely obsolete. Since 1970, various governments have, on six occasions, failed in their attempts to revise this Act. I think you will agree that protection of salaries in the case of corporate bankruptcy or receivership is an area where reform is badly needed, because workers are always hardest hit when factories close down. Any money they do receive is often paid many months later and generally represents only a small percentage of the amount owing.
Often, in cases of bankruptcy, the assets are not sufficient to pay secured creditors, so that there is no money left to pay the salaries of workers.
Mr. Speaker, improvements to this legislation have been in the works for twenty years, and during that time, just imagine how many workers, suddenly were out of a job that gave them a good living, lost their last week's wages!
Salary Insurance Protection Fund
As it stands today, the Bankruptcy Act ranks wage claims just before unsecured creditors. This means that wage claims rank only fourth and cover only wages due for services rendered during the three months immediately preceding the bankruptcy. The maximum amount of such claims is only $500.
Furthermore, bankruptcy procedures may take a very long time. It often takes months and even years to wind up a bankruptcy. However, the worker who has just been laid off and is unemployed needs those wages more than ever before. Unfortunately, the existing legislation does not provide for any compensation during that period.
Mr. Speaker, the inadequacy of these provisions has been an acknowledged fact for some time. Unfortunately, nothing has been done to remedy the problem. On May 5, 1975, Bill C-60 was tabled in the House of Commons. It proposed to give wages priority over any other secured or non-secured creditors, up to a total of $2,000 per employee. This kind of privileged treatment, known as top priority, would have given wage claims absolute priority, in other words, priority over any and all secured debts.
In its report on Bill C-60, the standing Senate committee responsible for bankruptcy indicated that giving wages top priority would substantially disrupt the business credit system. There are several reasons why the top priority clause is not the best way to protect wage-earners' rights. First of all, the clause would not guarantee absolutely payment of wages owing by a bankrupt business. In fact, the remaining assets of a company might not be sufficient to cover total wage claims. Furthermore, top priority for wage-earners would not necessarely guarantee speedy payment. In fact, it might take quite sometime before wage claims could be paid, since the sale and disposal of the assets of a bankrupt company can be a very lengthy procedure.
Furthermore, the courts would have to settle disputes and solve problems, which would likely prolong the process. A clause giving this top priority would not ensure that the employee could immediately obtain the funds needed to hold out until he finds work. The top priority clause is also very inconvenient, administratively. All money paid to the employee would have to be taken from the amounts owed to secured creditors. They too have deadlines to meet and they want to be paid. Distributing the salary claims payable would require a very complicated formula. For these reasons and many others, the top priority clause, although very attractive at first glance, is not the best way to protect employees of a company that goes bankrupt.
This was admitted by the Senate Committee, which recommended as an alternative the creation of a government-managed fund under the Bankruptcy Act to guarantee payment of wages owed when an employer declares bankruptcy. This proposal of a managed fund seems to have had the support of the Government of the time. The then-Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who is here today, the Hon.

May 20, 1988
Salary Insurance Protection Fund
Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), said, "If it can be shown to be justified, a funded insurance formula would obviously be the most desirable solution." However, nothing was done at the time. Bill C-12, presented in 1980, was another attempt to reform the Bankruptcy Act. In 1981, a committee chaired by Mr. Raymond Landry, now Dean of the Faculty of Law at the University of Ottawa and former Bankruptcy Superintendent, was charged with finding ways to protect employees.
In its report presented in October 1981, the Landry Committee recommended creating an employee protection fund. Despite the recommendations of the Landry Committee, Bill C-17, presented in 1984, contained essentially the same provisions concerning employees as Bill C-12. However, it was later amended to give priority to salary claims. Since Bill C-17 died on the Order Paper, we are still left with this old 1949 law, which, as I already said, protects employees very badly. It is precisely because I feel that this situation cannot continue that I have moved my motion.
In 1984, employees of bankrupt companies lost about $10 million in wages. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, how frustrating it must be for a worker to lose not only his job but even the wages earned over the previous weeks?
What impact does this have on the lives of the spouse, the children and the friends? If it's a company which provided a high percentage of the area's jobs, have you thought of the impact on local businesses? If there is no solution in view in that kind of a situation, then anxiety, terror, anger set into people's minds. This is generally what happens, and it becomes a tragedy. Sometimes, workers learn through the media that their business has been forced into bankrusptcy by a creditor. And the same evening the door is locked-no more pay, no more jobs! Sometimes, the misery last longer. A first pay cheque bounces, and as things go at the bank, the second goes through-the company makes promises, they ask for some time, one cheque goes through-two, three or six weeks go by, with every one on eages, and it happens again. What kind of an atmosphere does that create in a home? It must be kept in mind, Mr. Speaker, that we are living in 1988. At any rate, whether employees learn of their plight suddenly or they started wondering a few weeks or a few months earlier, the result is always the same. With the loss of job, the loss of earned income, it is the last straw.
Often the average worker will make small purchases on credit, especially in small towns where everyone knows everybody else, indicating to the store owner he will pay up on his next pay day. And all of a sudden his pay cheque bounces at the bank because the company is no longer solvent. You can imagine what kind of mess that worker finds himself in.
Hon. Members no doubt will recall Maislin Transport's demise in March 1984. That was a very good example of the lack of protection afforded by the Bankruptcy Act in the area of wage claims. More than 1,000 workers at that time went through hard times and sustained substantial financial losses.
All the 1160 Quebec and Ontario workers of that company could finally obtain in settlement of their wage claims was a meagre 35 cents on the dollar. To allow the same situation to happen again is simply unacceptable.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger), on March 21, 1984, said in this House, and I quote: "Recent events surrounding the Maislin bankruptcy settlement of unpaid employee's back salaries poignantly illustrate the immediate urgency for a new Bankruptcy Act providing wage protection for workers".
During the last election, Mr. Speaker, I met people who had suffered as a result of these corporate bankruptcies. In my riding as in all the other ridings in Canada, unfortunately, bankruptcies happen much too often. In the Drummond riding, some workers have incurred great losses. In August 1984, I was advised that a group of workers who had lost their jobs nearly one year before because of a bankruptcy, had received none of the wages they were entitled to. Yet, it was a supposedly prosperous business which had gone bankrupt and lost $5 million.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that in the Drummond riding, between 1981 and 1984, over 1,500 industrial jobs were lost because of corporate bankruptcies. I remember that during the last election quite a number of Saint-Cyrille-de-Wendover owners with very large farms had gone bankrupt. As you know, today, our farmers investments are enormous. Each of these farms is worth over $1 million. Between 1981 and 1984, 40 per cent of the farm bankruptcies were in Central Quebec. You will understand that if we add these jobs lost to the 1,500 which I have just mentioned, it is a fairly enormous proportion. How much money do all these salaries lost combined represent? And how much distress was caused because the legislation was entirely inadequate?
You appreciate now the reason why I moved this motion and its importance, Mr. Speaker. A salary insurance protection fund would be a good social policy.
If I may, I should like to refer to only two cases of corporate bankrupcies. There is the case of Sincere Manufacturing Inc., a jeans manufacturer whose 300 employees agreed in 1982 to plow back into their company their vacation pay worth more than $80,000. They thought their gesture would help their company with its debt problems. Despite this, the company went into bankruptcy for some $700,000 and, a few weeks later, the employees lost everything: their money, their job, even their jeans.
The same thing happened in the case of Destel Inc., makers of kitchen-cabinets. After a period of substained growth, the company decided to reinvest more than a million dollars in a major project. The 1982 recession hit hard this industrial sector, and within 15 months, the company went into bankruptcy for 2.5 million dollars. Despite a recovery plan and the involvement of 125 workers, the employees lost their jobs and their money.
May 20, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada, of Quebec and of Drummondville should not have to face such situations. The British North America Act of 1867 gives Parliament the right to legislate in matters concerning and I quote, "bankruptcy and insolvency". As I mentioned, however, in this area, the federal Government has only enacted the Bankruptcy Act which, to say the least, is outdated. That is why some provinces, given this legislative void, have tried to protect the rights of wage-earners by enacting legislation concerning receivership and bankruptcy.
In 1975, the Office de la construction du Quebec set up a fund to guarantee the payment of wages in the event of bankruptcies, insolvencies, disposal of personal assets and proposals of arrangements. This fund is financed by Canadian employers throughout Canada. Considering that there are approximately 12 million workers in this country, a contribution of about $2 per year by both employees and employers would be enough, whatever the industry, to create an insurance fund of some $50 million.
I suggest that there seems to be a consensus throughout Canada concerning this. Already, a number of provincial Governments have taken action, Manitoba and Ontario for instance. This trend can also be found at the international level. More and more industrialized nations have combined their priority status of salary claim scheme with another scheme providing for salary insurance protection for the payment of wages and other claims. Now over 20 industrialized nations have funds of this type.
Are we less civilized or compassionate than France or England? Most other industrialized nations have already taken steps to deal with salary protection in the event of a bankruptcy. Although it has been faced with this problem for a long time, Canada is still far behind, so far in fact that a number of provinces had to somewhat make up for that delay.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is time for us to remedy the situation. The time has come to implement a scheme to protect workers when their employers go bankrupt.
In view of the opinion expressed by several Parliamentary commissions and committees, both federal and provincial, in view of the leadership shown by member countries of the European Economic Community and the trend which already exists at the provincial level, it seems obvious that the best way to provide this protection is through the establishment of a salary insurance protection fund.
That is what I suggested in my motion, Mr. Speaker. This fund could be financed equally through contributions from both employers and employees and to achieve this aim, the amount of theses contributions does not need to be high. Red tape could be avoided by having the Unemployment Insurance Commission administer the fund. The UIC has the administrative mechanisms required to do the job and, as it happens, it already administers the Farm Credit Corporation AGR-3235 program under which a farmer is eligible for a sizeable amount the very day he declares bankruptcy. He also gets assistance,
Salary Insurance Protection Fund
training and counselling provided by a manpower centre consultant. The man goes right back to work and cannot be said to be flat broke, Mr. Speaker.
In conclusion, 1 believe the establishment of such a fund would make it possible to achieve most of the objectives. Payments would be guaranteed and made quickly, and fund administration would be simple and not costly. In addition, any priority given to wage claims would not really prejudice the availability of credit for Canadian companies.
Mr. Speaker, this problem is harmful to millions of Canadian workers, and it can be solved without upsetting everything. We must dust off our antiquated bankruptcy legislation and give Canadian workers the protection they deserve.
This Government is on the verge of doing whatever is necessary to overhaul the bankruptcy legislation, and I would suggest that my motion is one of the major elements of the reform. I am confident it will rally the support of all Hon. Members.
[DOT]	(1410)

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the Hon. Member For Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) on his resolution. I want to thank him for bringing it forward because it is very important. We are dealing with a very antiquated bankruptcy law one which goes back to 1949. There have been many attempts in the past to try to bring amendments to the law or to revamp the bankruptcy legislation. This has not been done because it always seems to fall between the cracks at the end of a parliamentary session or what have you. Especially in the 1980s many employees have through no fault of their own lost everything. As the Hon. Member has said, social pressures happen to a family when a bankruptcy occurs, which are very serious.
[DOT]	(1420)
In the last six months, 10 firms in my community have gone bankrupt. There has been absolutely no evidence of any kind of help for the employees involved, and certainly they are lowest on the priority list. There is no guarantee that they will get anything. It seems to me that it would make an awful lot of sense to look at some kind of legislation that would protect salaries.
New bankruptcy legislation should establish some kind of special salary protection fund and compensate workers for wages lost due to bankruptcies. When a company starts going into bankruptcy, the situation in the workplace is not always pleasant and there is a tremendous amount of tension. It becomes impossible for employees to put a little more effort into their jobs because their own worries and anxieties about what can happen to them take away from trying to save the companies involved. If the employees could put all their energies into trying to save the companies knowing that there was protection, it would be a great help.

May 20, 1988
Salary Insurance Protection Fund
France and Sweden have salary protection insurance schemes and it does not cost very much. It does not cost very much but it does work. If something like that could be implemented in Canada, I think this Parliament could be very proud of itself.
Canadian legislation does not see working people as a high priority. The bankruptcy law was brought in in 1949 and ignored the needs of the employees when companies went bankrupt.
In my community, major plants have closed, and we are still waiting for the Government to bring forward some kind of legislation that will help older workers. For those who are between 45 and 55 years of age, it is often very hard to get back into the workforce after jobs disappear. We as legislators have to deal with the majority of the people, and the majority of the people in Canada are working people. Certainly our laws should protect those people. We would do this if this resolution were implemented into legislation.
This is something New Democrats have been looking for over the years. In 1980, a Senate committee recommended that kind of legislation. Again, it fell between the cracks. I suppose that the Parliament of the day prorogued and by the time the new Parliament came in, it was no longer a priority.
Again, I would like to commend my hon. colleague for bringing forward what I think is a really important issue and something that should become a priority of this Parliament. It would not be very difficult to implement quite quickly legislation that would protect workers. It would not take very long to get the agreement of all Parties in the House on this. There are some things we do not agree on, but I think we could get agreement on something like this and quickly pass it. We would be leaving a legacy in that for the first time in 40 years, we would bring forward this kind of an amendment. It would not be very difficult to do, but it would change the lives of many working people.
In February of 1987, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) introduced a Bill to change the priority of payments of claims so that wages and salaries of employees would be protected to a limit of $9,000. This resolution calls for something like a national insurance fund paid for by all employers in Canada. It would not cost very much, and they could get a very good return on this investment. When things get tense in the workplace, employees are more productive if they are secure.
I have read editorials in Canadian newspapers dealing with how antiquated our bankruptcy laws are and how important it is to protect employees. Such legislation, however, still has not come forward. I certainly think that such legislation is long overdue.
I do not think that we would see any major opposition to such a proposal from employers. There have been enough hills and valleys in Canadian business life in this last decade that the employers realize the kinds of risks they take. It is
important that they are able to protect their employees. As well, employers can be fairly open with their employees about the risks they are taking if they know that security exists, and it would be easier to build a team spirit which is so often important, particularly for small business.
With such legislation, not only would we help employees but we would reinforce the attitude that people are important, we do not simply treat them as commodities and then toss them aside when companies go bankrupt. We would be saying that our public policy cares about people who work and respects the dignity of work. We think it is important that that kind of attitude should exist.
I see in this resolution something that would have protected many people in my riding. I hope that we do not stop at bankruptcy but look at programs that provide assistance when plants are closed as well. Many plants in my riding have been closed, including Firestone, and now another one. I do not think the workers there will get benefits. Canada Packers in Winnipeg closed as well and the workers' severance pay has been cut off. Again, we have the attitude that the workers are not important, and I do not think that that is a Canadian value. The Canadian value is to treat people with dignity, and we want to make sure that when that work ceases through no fault of their own, the workers can continue on in some way.
Very often, homes are lost, families are dislocated and there is a tremendous amount of social pressure. That is what happens when employment is lost. We need some way to bridge that, and I think the resolution the Hon. Member has put forward is the first attempt to bridge that gap.
On behalf of the New Democratic Party, I want to say that we would support any kind of legislation that would flow from this resolution. It would be a step forward. However, I would ask the Hon. Member to support us when we deal with severance pay legislation and older worker readjustment programs. I see those as part and parcel of sudden unemployment.
Many people in my riding have applied for work, but because they are older, people would not hire them. They have given up and have become social dependents. That is not what we want to see when people have put 30 or 35 years of work into society.
I would conclude by saying that this is a first step in very important amendments to the Bankruptcy Act. The entire Act must be revamped because it is archaic. It was antiquated when it was brought in, and I do not think this Government has to feel responsible for that, but I would certainly like to see it do something about it. This resolution is an important amendment that could be brought in very quickly.

Mr. Speaker, let me take a few minutes to congratulate the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) who tabled today what I consider to be a very important motion.
May 20, 1988

You know, Mr. Speaker, that for several years several members from all political parties have addressed the issue and it is well known that the Liberal Party has always turned a deaf ear to the recommendations made in this Chamber.
So, I will not be long, Mr. Speaker, for I know that after a certain time this motion cannot be passed. I will sit down with great pleasure and as the seconder of the motion, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault), and I wish him luck with it.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to congratulate my colleague from Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) for his motion to the effect that the Government should consider the advisibility of establishing a salary insurance protection fund, responsible for ensuring that workers of a bankrupt business will get the salaries owed to them.
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to say that I agree completely with my colleague, that the present bankruptcy legislation is obsolete giving no adequate protection to the worker whose employer is bankrupt. I agree with my colleague on another point: the absolute priority is not a practical solution for reasons he mentionned.
As to the solution he puts forward today, namely the establishment of a salary protection fund for workers, it is along the same lines as the solution recommended by the Senate committee which examined previous legislation and it is also similar to the solution put forward by the Advisory committee on Bankruptcy and Insolvency in its report published in January 1988, and to what the Government will propose.
Although we can say now that the details concerning the operation of the workers protection fund still needs some refinement, the protection of workers is paramount in the reform of the Bankruptcy Act which the Government is about to table.
Salary Insurance Protection Fund
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I can say that the Government is not prepared to let the bill end up where the six others did. We are now consulting all interested parties, among others the provincial and territorial governments, the Canadian Federation of Small Business, the Canadian Bar Association, and the ACEF of Quebec. These consultations will enable us to put the finishing touches and, hopefully, the bill will be tabled in the not too distant future.
Mr. Speaker, I might add that the bill the Government has in mind will not be a major overhaul of the legislation, but for openers it will deal with five or six issues which we think are much more urgent, so perhaps I might just mention them: first, protection for wage earners; second, secured creditors and receiverships; trade reorganizations; consumer arrangements and bankruptcies; preferred claims, including those of the Crown and, finally, amendments of a technical nature.
Mr. Speaker, such are the priorities of this Government, and I can say how very pleased I am that the Hon. Member chose to present this motion to the House. I hope the Bill will be up for consideration as soon as possible.
